trov-abuse-limits.title: Abuse limits: what a stranger with an account cannot do
trov-abuse-limits.body:
# Abuse limits: what a stranger with an account cannot do

Source: `docs/architecture/abuse-limits.md`, `src/platform/limits.ts` (every number), `src/notifications/resend.ts` (the From header). Tests: `test/abuse-limits.test.ts`.

## Why this exists

Anyone with a GitHub account, or a Google account with a verified address, can sign in and create one Free organization they own. This doc is everything that stands between that and Trov being used to send mail, fill storage or look people up.

## Per-person rate limits

One global table, `abuse_counters (subject, action, bucket, count, last_at)`. Taking one unit is **one statement** — an upsert that only counts while the window has room — so two racing requests cannot both take the last unit. It uses D1 only.

| `LIMITS` key | Limit | Counted on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `invite` | 50 per person per UTC day | creating and resending invitations, across every org |
| `test_send` | 20 per person per day | a notification test send |
| `email_change` | 5 per person per day | changing a notification address |
| `avatar_upload` | 20 per person per day | uploading a profile photo |
| `org_logo_upload` | 20 per person per day | uploading an organization image |
| `checkout` | 10 per person per day | starting a Stripe checkout |
| `support` | 10 per person per day | a signed-in support report |
| `support_anon_ip` | 3 per client address per day | a signed-out support report |
| `support_anon_all` | 50 per day, everyone together | all signed-out support reports |
| `handle_check` | 60 per caller per UTC hour | checking whether a handle or org slug is free |

How they behave:

- A refusal is a **429** `{ "error": "rate_limited", "retry_after": <seconds> }` with a `Retry-After` header. It writes nothing.
- The subject is the **person**, never the org, so creating more orgs multiplies nothing. A handle rename carries the counters.
- A superadmin is exempt and not counted.
- The role gate runs first: a refused non-admin spends nothing.
- A daily cron deletes old counters.

**To add a limit:** add a key to `LIMITS`; in the route, after validation and the role gate, write `const refused = await rateLimited(c, "<key>"); if (refused) return refused;`; and add a row to the table in the area doc.

Separately, each org is capped by its **plan**: people, repositories, environments, stored artifact bytes, each person's agent connections, and AI summaries per month. See the plans doc.

## Mail: an org contributes a display name, nothing else

One mail account and one verified domain send every org's mail, and any org admin can edit their org's sender setting. So:

- `deliveryFor` is the only way an **org's** mail leaves the Worker, and it builds the From header itself: `<name> <hello@trov.dev>`. Whatever address a stored value carries is dropped.
- The platform's own mail (the grant notice and the support notice) leaves through `platformDeliveryFor`.
- The sender **name** is restricted (`senderNameProblem`): 1–64 ASCII letters, digits, spaces and a few safe punctuation marks. No quotes, angle brackets, `@` or line breaks. No name containing "trov" except exactly `Trov`. A stored name that fails is sent as `Trov`.
- Every subject is flattened to one line.

## The signed-out contact form

`POST /api/support/public` is the one write a visitor can make without signing in. It stores a support report and mails the operator. What bounds it:

- **It cannot send mail to a third party.** Trov sends nothing to the address typed — no confirmation, no copy. The address is only the Reply-To on the operator's notice.
- **Per client address:** three a day. The limiter never sees the IP; its subject is a keyed hash, and no IP is stored on the report.
- **A global cap:** 50 a day in total. Past it the form tells people to write to `hello@trov.dev`.
- **A honeypot and a minimum time on the form.** These keep cheap scripts out; the two limits stop determined ones.
- **Strict shape:** JSON only, every field capped, one plain address.
- **The notice treats typed text as hostile:** everything is HTML-escaped and the only links are Trov's own.
- **The address stays unverified**, and is never written to `persons` or `identities`.

Residual: the operator's inbox can still get up to 50 unwanted notices a day, each with an attacker-chosen Reply-To. That is why the address is labelled unverified everywhere.

## The notification address is not an oracle

`persons.email` is where a person's digests go. It is **not** an identity. Sign-in and invitations match on `identities.verified_email` — what a provider asserted — never on it. It is not unique, and saving an address that is on someone else's row gives exactly the same response as any other, so the route cannot be used to test whether an address is registered.

## Residual risks — not addressed

These are open decisions for the owner, not solved problems:

1. **Notification addresses are unverified.** A person can point their address at someone else and send them a test send or a digest of their own org's content.
2. **GitHub identities are pinned on first use.** `identities.provider_uid` is bound at an identity's next GitHub sign-in. If a member's login was renamed away and re-registered before then, the new holder would sign in as them.
3. **An invitation by GitHub login names a login, not an account.** Whoever holds the login at sign-in may accept it. Invite by login only someone about to sign in, and revoke stale invitations.
4. **`org_login_map` attributes by login.** A login that changes hands mis-attributes that login's events inside the org. It grants no access.
5. **The invitation mail carries text a stranger chooses** — the org's name, the inviter's name, the invitee's name — to any address, from the platform's address, 50 a day per person. It is all escaped and the only link is the site root, but the words are theirs.
6. **Shared platform resources.** Summaries for every org use the Worker's one Gemini key (capped per org per month by plan). The repo cron's subrequest budget is shared by rotation. `/mcp` and the tenant routes are metered but not limited. D1 rows are not capped.
7. **Open Free organizations.** One owned Free org per account, but accounts are free to make, so a determined person can make many — each bounded by Free's limits and the per-person rate limits.

trov-artifacts.title: Artifacts and doc images
trov-artifacts.body:
# Artifacts and doc images

Source: `docs/architecture/artifacts.md`, `docs/artifact-contract.md` (the contract for agents — read it before a first artifact write), `src/tools/artifacts.ts`, `src/tools/artifacts-agent.ts`, `src/artifacts/`, `shared/artifacts-core.ts`, `web/src/artifacts.ts`.

## What an artifact is

An artifact is one self-contained page an agent or a person produced — a design, spec, report, diagram, image, PDF or file — stored and versioned in Trov and linked to the work it came from. It lives under Knowledge › Artifacts (`#artifacts`, `#artifacts/<slug>`), and a ticket's detail shows its artifacts.

Artifacts are **direct** writes, not staged. The human confirmation is **ratify**.

## Kinds and storage

| Kinds | Cap | Stored in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Text: `html`, `markdown`, `svg`, `mermaid` | 750 KB of UTF-8 | the `content` column in D1 |
| Binary: `image` (png, jpeg, gif, webp), `pdf`, `file` | 10 MB | the R2 bucket `ARTIFACTS_BUCKET`, at `artifacts/<sha256>` |

Tables (migration `0030_artifacts`): `artifact_pages`, `artifact_versions`, `artifact_links`, `artifact_upload_tokens`, `artifacts_fts`.

The vocabulary, caps, status rules and wire DTOs live once in `shared/artifacts-core.ts` (zod-free, so the SPA can import it). The repository is `src/tools/artifacts.ts`. Every surface calls it; none re-implements a rule.

## Status and visibility rules

- Create makes version 1 as `draft`. Anyone who can read the page can move it between `draft` and `published`.
- Every later version is `published` and clears any ratification.
- A version with the same sha256 as the current one is a no-op (`unchanged`).
- Only the **author** may set a page `private`. A private page is readable and writable only by its author.
- A binary page whose upload has not landed exists to no reader.
- A private page, an un-uploaded page, a deleted page and a missing slug all return **one byte-identical not-found** on every surface. `test/artifacts.security-access.test.ts` pins this.

Slugs are one namespace, so allocating `<slug>-2` does reveal that a hidden page with that title exists — never its content or author. This is a known, accepted leak.

## Ratify — the human gate

`draft` → `published` → `ratified`. Only `ratified` is team-confirmed.

`POST /api/artifacts/:slug/ratify {version}` is session-cookie only, works only on the latest version of a published page, and refuses any request carrying an `Authorization` header. There is no MCP ratify tool. Never describe a `published` artifact as agreed.

## Delete is soft

`POST /api/artifacts/:slug/delete` stamps `deleted_at` and `deleted_by` and drops the search row. Every version, link and the R2 bytes stay, so restore is lossless.

- Only the page's author or an org admin may delete, and only a page they can see.
- The slug stays reserved: a new page with the same title gets `<slug>-2`.
- `POST /api/artifacts/:slug/restore` brings it back.
- Both are cookie-only. There is no MCP delete.

## HTTP

`src/artifacts/routes.ts`, mounted at `/api/artifacts`, session cookie: list (filters for area, kind, author, status, sprint, ticket, text), get, create, PATCH, add version (full content, or `old_str` / `new_str` which must match exactly once), add and remove links, diff, ratify, delete, restore.

`POST /api/artifacts/fetch` backs the From-URL tab: https only, private and loopback addresses refused, every redirect re-checked, text only, nothing stored.

### Two token routes outside the session gate

These sit in `src/index.ts` before the session-gated app:

- **Upload** — `PUT /api/artifacts/upload/:token`. Single use, five minutes, bound to the principal, page, kind, size and sha256. Stored only as a hash.
- **Agent download** — `GET /api/artifacts/download/:token`. A stateless HMAC token, five minutes, reusable. The page's visibility is re-checked at download.

### The raw route

`GET /raw/a/:slug` is what the SPA frames. HTML and SVG get a strict content security policy plus `sandbox allow-scripts`, so an artifact runs at an opaque origin with no network access. The SPA frames html as a sandboxed `<iframe src>` — never `srcdoc`, never `allow-same-origin` — and inlines SVG only through `sanitizeSvg` (DOMPurify).

## MCP tools

For every principal, in `src/tools/artifacts-agent.ts`:

- `artifact_list` — the pages you can see.
- `artifact_get` — text content inline up to 64 KB (`ARTIFACT_INLINE_MAX`); for every kind a signed `download_url` plus `sha256` and `size_bytes` to verify against.
- `upload_asset` — creates a page. Text kinds send `content`; binary kinds send `size_bytes` and `sha256` and get back an `upload_url` to PUT the exact bytes to.
- `artifact_update` — a new version.

All of them return `warnings` — never a rejection — when content calls something only claude.ai provides, or is a bundled export that must be flattened first.

`query` has an `artifact` type, `get_ticket` lists a ticket's visible artifacts, and `record_session` accepts `artifact_links`, applied as direct writes after the batch.

The `artifacts` skill is the procedure: find, pull into `.trov/artifacts/<slug>/v<n>.<ext>`, verify the hash, serve an html page locally, link, and publish only when asked.

## Doc images

A doc embeds an image as `![alt](/img/<sha256>)`.

- **Storage.** One `doc_images` row per sha256 (png, jpeg, gif or webp, up to 10 MB); the bytes are in R2 at `doc-images/<sha256>`. They are immutable and never deleted, so a promoted version renders the same forever.
- **Upload.** The same MCP tool, `upload_asset` with `destination: "doc"`. It returns the reference and, if the bytes are not stored yet, an `upload_url`. The PUT is the same upload route as artifacts.
- **The gate.** A doc proposal that references an image not yet uploaded, or any other image source, is `refused` (see the ingestion gate doc).
- **Serving.** `GET /img/<sha>` on the session-gated app. An agent cannot read it with a bearer.
- **Web.** Images in a doc open in a lightbox. Review's Rendered view outlines added images green and removed ones red.

There is no web upload for doc images yet (agents only, by decision) and no garbage collection.

## Deferred on purpose

External share links, per-person sharing, a separate raw-content subdomain, and PDF text extraction for search.

trov-auth-identity-people.title: Auth, identity and people
trov-auth-identity-people.body:
# Auth, identity and people

Source: `docs/architecture/auth-identity-people.md`, `src/auth/` (`onboard.ts`, `oauth.ts`, `oauth-routes.ts`, `oauth-pages.ts`, `persons.ts`, `tokens.ts`), `src/data/bearer.ts`, `src/github-hook.ts`, `src/tools/people.ts`, `shared/people.ts`.

## Three auth classes — do not add a fourth

| Class | Who | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Session cookie | people | the Hono app (every route except the public auth paths passes `sessionGate`) |
| Bearer | agents | `/mcp` only |
| HMAC | GitHub | the webhooks |

The Hono app is cookie-only. Two signed-token exceptions — the `/u/` unsubscribe link and the artifact upload and download routes — sit in `src/index.ts` before the session gate.

## Signing in

Anyone with a GitHub account, or a Google account whose address Google has verified, can sign in and so create an account. There is no org gate and no invitation gate. What that person can then do is covered by the abuse-limits and organizations docs.

Both providers use OAuth with PKCE and feed **one fork**, `completeSignIn` in `src/auth/onboard.ts`:

1. A known identity gets a session.
2. A verified email that matches a person links the new identity to that person and gets a session.
3. Anyone else goes to onboarding. The person row is created only on `POST /auth/onboard`, with a handle and a color.

A Google address Google has not verified is refused in the callback, before the fork. A person can attach the second provider in Settings; the last identity cannot be unlinked.

Onboarding creates a **person, never a membership**. A new person is in no org until they accept an invite or create one.

**Docs disagree here.** `docs/architecture/data-layer.md` still says a new Google identity reaches onboarding "only with a pending invite". `auth-identity-people.md` and the code in `src/auth/onboard.ts` say any verified Google account does (open Google sign-up shipped in release 0.23). The code wins.

## Bearer tokens and MCP OAuth

A bearer is either a pasted per-person token (prefix `canopy_mcp_`, stored hashed) or an OAuth access token (prefix `canopy_oat_`). The old product name is kept in these prefixes on purpose. Both resolve to a connection in `resolveBearerConnection` in `src/data/bearer.ts`. OAuth is how a bearer is *obtained*, not a fourth class. Which organization a call acts in is its own doc (MCP connection modes).

The Settings UI is OAuth-only. Nothing in the SPA mints or lists pasted tokens any more, but the token routes remain, so a token already in use keeps working.

Trov runs its own OAuth server (migration `0029_oauth`):

- Standard discovery metadata and dynamic client registration for public clients.
- Authorization code with S256 PKCE.
- A server-rendered consent page shown on **every** authorization. It says who is approving, offers "Not you? Sign out", and asks how the connection picks an organization.
- Access tokens last one hour. Refresh tokens rotate; reusing an old one outside a 60-second window revokes the whole grant.
- `pruneOAuth` rides the repo cron and deletes spent codes and expired tokens. Grants are never deleted.

`/mcp` is bearer-only. Its 401 carries a `WWW-Authenticate` header pointing at the resource metadata, which is how Claude Code discovers sign-in. A fresh `McpServer` is built per request; the handler is stateless.

Every OAuth endpoint answers an unexpected error with a 503, never a 500.

Settings › MCP access lists a person's connections under **Connected apps**, with Revoke and a **Change organization…** dialog. Those routes (`/auth/oauth-grants…`) are cookie-only, never MCP tools.

## The GitHub webhook

`POST /webhook/github/:hookId` (`src/github-hook.ts` → `src/webhook.ts`). The hook id is the repo's `org_repos.id`.

- A delivery authenticates with an HMAC-SHA256 signature over the raw body, against **that repo's** stored webhook secret.
- It must name that repo, or it is ignored (202).
- A bad or missing signature, an unknown hook id and a suspended org all get the same bare 401 with nothing written, so hook ids cannot be probed.
- The writer is the fixed principal `github-webhook`.

The GitHub App has one webhook of its own, `POST /webhook/github/app` (see the GitHub App doc).

## Identity — persons, not logins

- `persons` (handle as primary key; name, color, email) is the root. The handle is chosen at first sign-in and can be renamed in Settings.
- `renamePerson` rewrites every stored handle atomically using `HANDLE_COLUMNS`. Every `*_by`, owner or author column is a handle and **must** be listed there.
- `identities(provider, subject) → person` holds the GitHub login and the Google subject.
- An event's GitHub login resolves to a person at read time (`resolvePersonForLogin`). An unmapped login raises an `identity_tasks` row; an admin links it to a handle in Org settings › Members, or discards it (soft, and it stays discarded).
- Admin is the org role on the membership. There is no allowlist of handles.

## People profiles

Three optional fields per person, written directly by `src/tools/people.ts`: an avatar, a role and responsibilities.

- **Avatar.** One rule, `avatarSrc` in `shared/people.ts`: an uploaded avatar outranks the provider picture; otherwise initials. Every DTO sends the picture already resolved, so a new surface must go through `avatarSrc` too. A person uploads only their own (`POST /api/people/me/avatar`, at most 2 MB, type checked by magic bytes, stored in R2).
- **Role and responsibilities are admin-set.** `PUT /api/people/:handle` is admin-only; the person themselves cannot change them.
- **`responsibilities` is never rendered.** It goes only to admins and to the MCP tool `list_people`.
- **MCP gets one read**, `list_people`, returning handle, name, role and responsibilities. There is no people write. A null means unknown — never guess.

There is no People screen and no profile page. A click on anyone's name or avatar opens the **person card** modal (`web/src/profile.ts`). A clickable person always goes through `web/src/people.ts`. A card that opens something else uses `hitArea` — never a button inside a button.

trov-data-layer.title: The data layer: tenant and platform contexts
trov-data-layer.body:
# The data layer: tenant and platform contexts

Source: `docs/architecture/data-layer.md`, `src/data/` (`context.ts`, `sql.ts`, `platform-sql.ts`, `gate.ts`, `bearer.ts`, `secrets.ts`, `legacy.ts`), `src/platform/jobs.ts`, `src/repo/dispatch.ts`, `test/data-layer.static.test.ts`.

## The rule

Trov is multi-tenant: many organizations share one D1 database. Isolation rests on one rule — **every tenant statement binds `ctx.orgId`** — and on D1 being reachable only inside `src/data/`. Nothing else in `src/` names `D1Database`, `env.DB`, `.prepare(` or `.batch(`.

## Two contexts

| | Type | Built by | Query surface |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tenant data | `TenantContext { orgId, userId, role, via }` | `resolveTenant` (slug + membership), `resolveTenantById`, `resolveSoleTenant`, `liveTenants`, `systemTenant(p, orgId, actor)` | `src/data/sql.ts` |
| Platform data | `PlatformContext { actor }` | `platform(env, actor)` | `src/data/platform-sql.ts` |

Both surfaces export the same helpers: `first`, `all`, `run`, `stmt`, `batch`, `fanOut`, plus `nowIso`, `ph`, `chunked`.

- Every resolver is one statement and also checks `orgs.suspended_at`. A suspended org resolves for no one.
- A repository never builds a context. A module that needs both kinds takes the tenant context and receives the platform one as a parameter.
- `src/data/secrets.ts` is the only module that can reach a context's environment.

## Which tables are which

The lists are derived from the live schema: every table with an `org_id` column is org-keyed.

- **Tenant tables** — all content tables and their full-text tables, the per-user-per-org tables (`mcp_tokens`, `oauth_grants`, `notification_*`), and an org's configuration (`org_repos`, `org_environments`, `org_secrets`, `org_github_installations` and so on).
- **Platform-owned, org-keyed** — `memberships`, `org_invites`, `org_counters`, `org_usage_daily`, `org_admin_audit`.
- **Global** (no `org_id`) — `persons`, `identities`, `sessions`, `oauth_clients`, `oauth_tokens`, `orgs`, `platform_admins`, `cron_cursor`, `abuse_counters`, `sections`, `tags`, `org_grants`, `support_reports`.

## Writing a statement

- Write the predicate exactly `org_id = ?` (or `<alias>.org_id = ?`), bound from `ctx.orgId` — never a literal, never a request value. One per org-keyed table the statement touches, joins and subqueries included.
- Put the predicate in the statement text, not in a conditional clauses array.
- Every `INSERT` into an org-keyed table lists `org_id`; an upsert target names it.
- A lookup by a global id is `WHERE id = ? AND org_id = ?`, so another org's id reads as not found.
- Full-text: `org_id` is the last column, and every `MATCH` adds the org predicate.
- A handle from input that must be a person in the org goes through `requireMember(ctx, handle)`. Unknown, reserved and non-member all read the same.

## The static test

`test/data-layer.static.test.ts` reads the source text of `src/` and fails with a file, line, rule and statement:

1. No D1 access outside `src/data/`. No allowlist.
2. A tenant statement has `org_id` once per org-keyed table, in every insert column list and upsert target, never against a literal.
3. A platform statement names no tenant table, except a small allowlist in the test — each entry with its file, function and reason (cross-org retention sweeps, credential lookup by hash before any org is known, the superadmin's counts, a handle rename).
4. Table lists come from the live schema, so a new table is covered automatically.

It is a text heuristic, not a proof. The isolation tests (`test/isolation.*.test.ts`) are the behavioural half: write through org B, read through org A, expect nothing.

## A ticket's and a handoff's two ids

`tickets.number` and `handoffs.number` are allocated per org by a trigger from `org_counters`. **The wire's `id` is that number** — every route parameter, MCP argument and result, quick search, My Work and artifact link. The global row id never leaves the Worker. Sprints, comments and links have no per-org number.

Links the Worker hands out (an MCP result's `url`, a digest's deep link) are built in `src/tools/org-links.ts` from the context's org: `<origin>/<slug>/#…` for the app and `<origin>/api/o/<slug>/…` for tenant routes. (The area doc still shows the older `/o/<slug>/` app prefix; the code uses `/<slug>/`, and `/o/<slug>/…` is a 301 to it.)

## Routes and gates

Every session request passes `sessionGate`, then exactly one of:

| Path | Gate | Tenant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/api/o/:slug/*` | `tenantGate` | the org the path names, if the caller is a member; otherwise 404 (unknown slug, non-member and suspended all alike) |
| `/auth/*`, `/avatar/*`, `/api/orgs`, `/api/invites`, `/api/support`, `/api/platform/*` | none (person-level) | none: the caller's own person, or superadmin-only |
| every other path | `soleTenantGate` | the caller's **one** org — 409 `org_required` with none or several |

`soleTenantGate` is the default, so a route added without thought is tenant-gated, never open. It is a cut-over alias; the remaining cleanup phase deletes it.

- A tenant route is defined once and mounted twice — under `/api/o/:org` and at its old path. A handler reads `c.var.ctx`, never the path.
- Confirm verbs (promote, reject, ratify, publish) and the whole org surface refuse a request carrying an `Authorization` header (`cookieOnly`).
- A plan limit is checked in the repository with `requirePlan`; `app.onError` turns it into a 402 `plan_limit`.
- A route that sends mail, stores bytes or answers a lookup takes a rate-limit unit with `rateLimited(c, "<key>")`.

## Background jobs

No background entry point names an org. Each one enumerates the orgs through `src/platform/jobs.ts`, then works as that org's `systemTenant`:

- the repo cron (`handleRepoCron`) — every non-suspended org's environments and primary repo;
- the digest crons (`handleNotificationCron`);
- the webhooks — the org is found from the hook id or the App installation id;
- Poll now, Poll usage and Sync GitHub — the caller's org.

**The rotation dispatcher** (`src/repo/dispatch.ts`) turns each cadence into a job over units. One invocation serves units in order, starting after a stored cursor (`cron_cursor`), while the work still fits a subrequest budget (900 fetches) and a wall-clock budget (8 minutes). Each unit is total: it catches its own failure, records it on that org's integration row, and the loop moves on.

Credentials are resolved only in modules `src/mcp.ts` cannot reach, and passed down as parameters. `test/secrets.mcp.test.ts` enforces it.

## What is still org #1's alone

`src/data/legacy.ts` is the only file that names the first organization, for two things that predate orgs: the legacy `invites` table and the environment-secret fallback for that org's integrations. Callers are marked `// MT:`. The legacy `POST /webhook/github` route is the same kind of residue.

## Test helpers

`test/helpers/tenant.ts` has `systemCtx`, `tenantCtx`, `bearerCtx`, `mintTokenFor`, `ORG_A`, `ORG_B`. `test/isolation.http.test.ts` is generated from the Hono route registry: a route with no entry fails the suite, so add the entry with the route.

trov-deploy-runbook.title: Deploy runbook and production gotchas
trov-deploy-runbook.body:
# Deploy runbook and production gotchas

Source: `HANDOFF.md` (the repo's deploy runbook), `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/architecture/env.md`, `wrangler.toml`, `package.json`, the `ops` lines in `web/src/releases.ts`, and the owner's own verification where noted.

## What production is

One Cloudflare Worker named `trov`, on one origin (`https://trov.dev`), with the D1 database `trov` and the R2 bucket `trov-artifacts`. Deploys run through Cloudflare **Workers Builds**, connected to the GitHub repository `AndresL230/trov`.

## The commands

- `npm test` — the suite. The source of truth for "is it green".
- `npm run typecheck` — **not** part of `npm test`. Run it too.
- `npm run build:web` — builds the SPA into `web/dist`.
- `npm run deploy` — builds the SPA and runs `wrangler deploy`.
- `npm run db:migrate:local` / `npm run db:migrate:remote` — apply D1 migrations.
- `npm run deploy:preview` — applies migrations to the preview database and deploys a Preview.
- `npm run dev` — local Worker plus a watching web build. Never run `build:web` under a running `wrangler dev`; it empties `web/dist`.

## The gotchas — read these first

1. **A merge to `main` is a production deploy.** Workers Builds ships the Worker and applies new migrations. There is no staging step in between. After merging, verify the live bundle.

2. **A push of ANY branch currently applies that branch's new migrations to production.** Verified by the owner on 2026-10-09. The branch push does **not** deploy the Worker, but its migrations reach the production database. The mechanism is described in `env.md`: Cloudflare refuses `wrangler deploy` from a branch build but does not refuse `wrangler d1 migrations apply trov --remote`. The intended setup is that the non-production deploy command is `npm run deploy:preview`, which targets the separate `trov-preview` database. Until that is fixed, treat **pushing a branch that contains a new migration as a production schema change**: keep migrations additive, and do not push a draft migration.

3. **A secret change ships the latest uploaded build.** `wrangler secret put …` redeploys with whatever build was uploaded last — which may be a branch build, not `main`. Change a secret only when the latest build is the one you mean to run.

4. **A cron change does not deploy with the merge.** After merging a change to `[triggers] crons`, run `wrangler triggers deploy`. Also: Cloudflare cron weekdays are 1–7 or `SUN`–`SAT`, never 0, and a bad expression fails the deploy **after** the Worker has uploaded.

5. **Vars come from `wrangler.toml`.** A var changed only in the Cloudflare dashboard is undone by the next deploy.

6. **Running `wrangler … --remote` by hand** needs `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` set, or it fails with an authentication error.

## Migrations

`migrations/` is numbered, append-only D1 SQL. Each file's header says what it does and, where it has one, how to roll it back.

- **Never edit a migration production has recorded.** Add a new one.
- Numbers have gaps on purpose (there is no 0037–0040 and no 0050). Do not renumber.
- Multi-part migrations use marker lines that tests cut on.
- `0042_organizations` is the multi-tenancy migration: one all-or-nothing file that must stay under 100 KB, because it reaches D1 as one request. Its rollback is **generated** by `scripts/mt/build-rollback.py`, and CI fails if the generated file is stale.
- Where a release needs ordering, its `ops` lines say so. Release 0.25: apply `0051_mcp_connection_orgs` **before** the Worker that reads it.
- Every new table must be added to `scripts/seed/reset.mjs`, and a new handle column to `HANDLE_COLUMNS`.

## Shipping a pull request

1. Add your lines to the **top entry** of `web/src/releases.ts`: release notes in product words for users, `ops` deploy steps for whoever deploys, and patch lines ending `(#N)`.
2. The PR that merges a batch cuts the release: it sets the next `0.N` and the merge date. `main` never carries an "Unreleased" entry.
3. Update the matching file in `docs/architecture/` in the same PR when behaviour changes.
4. Merge. Then do the `ops` steps: secrets, `wrangler triggers deploy`, publishing the plugin.

The Claude Code plugin is distributed from the same repository (`plugins/trov/`, `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`), so plugin updates track `main`. Release 0.25 carries plugin 0.8.0.

## Rollback

- **Worker:** `wrangler rollback`.
- **Database, soon after a change:** D1 Time Travel. Note the bookmark *before* a risky migration (`npx wrangler d1 time-travel info <db>`), then `wrangler d1 time-travel restore <db> --bookmark=<it>`.
- **Database, later:** the by-hand rollback statements in the migration's header, where it has them.

A schema change that is not compatible with the old Worker must ship together with the new Worker, in a quiet window.

## First-time setup of a deployment

In short, from `HANDOFF.md`: create the R2 bucket before the first deploy that binds it; set `TROV_KEK` and keep a copy somewhere safe; confirm the **Workers Paid** plan, because the repo cron budgets 900 subrequests per invocation and the free plan allows 50; verify the sending domain before `NOTIFICATIONS_MODE` is `resend`; then follow the owner checklists in the GitHub App and billing docs.

## Do not

- Do not `git add -A` or `git add .` in the owner's checkout. Several untracked files are the owner's local files, including a production data dump. Stage explicit paths and run `git status --short` before every commit. Never read, move or delete those files.
- Do not activate the deferred seams (Cloudflare Queue, Vectorize).
- Do not rename the stored `canopy` identifiers: the `canopy_mcp_` / `canopy_oat_` token prefixes, the `canopy/*` commit-status contexts, the `canopy-health` / `canopy-metrics` user agents, and `tickets.source = 'canopy'`. They are contracts, not branding.

## Where `HANDOFF.md` is out of date

`HANDOFF.md` was written as a session handoff during the multi-tenancy work and has not been fully rewritten. Its checklists are still useful, but several statements no longer match production:

- It opens with "Nothing is merged or deployed" and describes the GitHub App, billing and per-seat Pro as unmerged. All of that has shipped; production is at release 0.25.
- It says the SPA lives at `/o/<slug>/` and that links are `<origin>/o/<slug>/#…`. The code serves the app at `/<slug>/` (`src/tools/org-links.ts`); the old form redirects.
- It says `wrangler.toml` has `NOTIFICATIONS_MODE = "local"`. It is `resend`.
- It describes Personal and Team plans with placeholder numbers. The plans are Free, Pro and Enterprise, as in `shared/plans.ts`.
- It says to delete the file before the branch merges; it is on `main`, and CLAUDE.md names it as the runbook.

Trust the code, `wrangler.toml` and the `ops` lines of the newest release over `HANDOFF.md`.

trov-docs-and-decisions.title: Docs and decisions: propose, promote, reject, ratify
trov-docs-and-decisions.body:
# Docs and decisions: propose, promote, reject, ratify

Source: `docs/architecture/ingestion-gate.md`, `docs/architecture/feed-and-search.md`, `src/consumer.ts`, `src/routes.ts`, `src/mcp.ts`, `src/tools/reads.ts`, `shared/vocabulary.ts`, the `trov` and `load-context` skills under `plugins/trov/skills/`.

## The rule

**Agents stage; humans confirm.** A doc edit or a decision an agent writes does not become team knowledge until a person confirms it. Every confirm verb is a session-cookie route and **never an MCP tool**. Those routes also refuse any request that carries an `Authorization` header (`cookieOnly` in `src/routes.ts`), so a bearer token cannot confirm even by calling the HTTP route directly.

## A doc's life

A doc is a row in `docs` plus its versions in `doc_versions`.

1. **Propose.** An agent calls `propose_doc_update` (or sends `doc_proposals` in a `record_session` batch). A person can stage a new doc from Docs › New doc (`POST /api/docs/propose`; an existing slug there is a 409). All three go through `ingestDocProposal` in the gate.
2. **Staged.** The gate writes a `doc_versions` row with status `staged`. The live doc is untouched: `current_version` does not move. A doc that has never been promoted has `current_version = 0` and an empty live body.
3. **Review.** The proposal appears in the Review screen (`#review`). `GET /proposals` returns the queue server-joined: staged versions newer than the live doc, with both bodies and the reconciler's metadata.
4. **Promote** — `POST /doc/:slug/promote`. Copies the staged version into the live doc and bumps `current_version`. Non-destructive: prior versions remain.
5. **Or reject** — `POST /doc/:slug/reject`. Flips the staged version to `rejected`. The row and its body remain. Idempotent.

Any member of the organization may promote or reject; it is not admin-only.

## What the reviewer sees

The gate computes these, so a reviewer does not have to trust the writer's own description:

- **`change_kind`** — `new`, `edit` or `rewrite`, from a line diff of the proposed body against the live one.
- **`base_version`** — the version the writer said it read. If the live doc has moved since, the edit is flagged as stale.
- **`low_confidence`** — set when a low-confidence proposal targets an existing doc. (Low confidence on a *new* slug goes to triage instead.)

Review offers the diff as unified, split, or a Rendered view; in Rendered, added images are outlined green and removed ones red.

## Classification

A doc has a `section`, which must be in the gate's vocabulary (`shared/vocabulary.ts`): `reference`, `context`, `decisions` or `needs-triage`. It also has a `space`: `technical` (the default) or `product`.

An out-of-vocabulary section routes the proposal to **Triage › Unplaced** (`#unplaced`), where a person assigns it — which re-runs it through the same gate — or discards it. Nothing is guessed.

`docs.owner` is the handle of whoever proposed the doc's **first** version. It is set once and never overwritten; `updated_by` is the last promoter.

## A decision's life

A decision (an ADR) is simpler: it has a status rather than versions.

1. **Draft.** An agent stages one through the gate (`ingestAdrDraft`) by sending `adr_drafts` in a `record_session` batch or to `/ingest`. There is no standalone MCP tool for a single decision draft.
2. **Ratify** — `POST /adr/:id/ratify` flips it to `ratified`.
3. **Or reject** — `POST /adr/:id/reject` flips it to `rejected`. The row remains.

Content-hash dedupe applies here too: an identical body for an existing decision is a no-op.

Decisions have no screen of their own. They appear in Review while they are drafts, and in search once ratified.

**A small inconsistency in the docs:** `ingestion-gate.md` says "`stage_adr` stages a draft". `stage_adr` is the internal writer's name; no MCP tool is registered under it. Over MCP, the route in is `record_session`.

## Authority flags

Every read result says how settled it is:

| Flag | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `live` | settled — trust it |
| `staged_pending` | a newer version is staged; the body you see is still the live one |
| `unpromoted` | exists only as staged content; never promoted |
| `draft` | an unratified decision |

Never present anything that is not `live` as established fact.

The MCP `query` tool includes staged content by default, flagged. The human search (`GET /search`) shows only settled content, and quick search withholds a never-promoted doc and a non-ratified decision entirely.

## Everything is soft

Rejecting a doc version or a decision, and every triage exit, is soft and audited. Nothing is hard-deleted, so a mistaken rejection loses nothing.

## How to propose well (for an agent)

1. **Orient first.** Run the `load-context` skill, or call `query` and `get_doc`. Never propose blind.
2. **Do not duplicate.** If a doc for the area exists, update it. Check `list_docs` — it lists staged-only docs too, with `current_version: 0`.
3. **Pass `base_version`** — the `current_version` you read.
4. **Use the vocabulary** for `section`, and pick the right `space`.
5. **Be honest about confidence.** `high` only for what you read in the code or the area doc directly.
6. **Images** must be uploaded first with `upload_asset` (`destination: "doc"`) and referenced as `![alt](/img/<sha256>)`. Anything else is refused.
7. **Write a real `change_summary`.** It is what the reviewer reads first.
8. **Check the outcome.** `written` with status `staged` is success. `unchanged` means the body was identical. `needs_triage` means fix the vocabulary or confidence. `refused` means fix the images. Do not resend blindly.

An unchanged body is dropped unless `force: true` is passed.

## Where a person reviews

Open the organization in the web app and go to **Review** in the sidebar: `https://trov.dev/<org-slug>/#review`. Items the gate could not place are under **Triage › Unplaced**: `https://trov.dev/<org-slug>/#unplaced`.

trov-environment.title: Environment: secrets, vars and bindings
trov-environment.body:
# Environment: secrets, vars and bindings

Source: `docs/architecture/env.md`, `wrangler.toml`, `.dev.vars.example`, `src/env.ts`. This doc lists **names only**. Secret values live in Cloudflare (`wrangler secret put …`) and, for local development, in `.dev.vars`, which is never committed and never to be copied anywhere.

## Bindings

| Binding | What | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DB` | D1 database `trov` | reached only inside `src/data/` |
| `ASSETS` | the built SPA (`web/dist`) | static assets |
| `ARTIFACTS_BUCKET` | R2 bucket `trov-artifacts` | binary artifacts, doc images, avatars, org images. The bucket must exist before the first deploy that carries the binding |

There is no `[ai]` block. Summaries call Gemini over plain REST with a key.

Two deferred seams exist only as `// SEAM:` comments and must **not** be activated: a Cloudflare Queue and Vectorize.

## Secrets

**Sign-in and sessions**

- `GITHUB_CLIENT_ID`, `GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET` — GitHub sign-in (the App's client).
- `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`, `GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET` — Google sign-in. Without the id, Google login answers 503.
- `COOKIE_SECRET` — signs the session cookie, and keys the signed links and sealed cookies.

**Encryption**

- `TROV_KEK` — the deployment's key-encryption key. Each org's stored integration credentials are envelope-encrypted under it. **Losing it loses every org's stored credentials.**

**The GitHub App**

- `GITHUB_APP_ID`, `GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` (the whole `.pem`), `GITHUB_APP_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. Missing the id, the key or the slug var means only the by-hand token path is offered. Nothing returns a 500.

**Summaries and mail**

- `GEMINI_API_KEY` — capture-time summaries of pull requests and issues. Absent → items show an excerpt and nothing is counted.
- `RESEND_API_KEY` — email delivery. Needed only when `NOTIFICATIONS_MODE` is `resend`.

**Billing**

- `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`, `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. Missing either → billing is off and every billing route answers 503.

**Legacy fallback for the first organization only**

- `GITHUB_SERVICE_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, `CF_ANALYTICS_TOKEN`, `CF_ANALYTICS_ACCOUNT_ID`, `RAILWAY_TOKEN_<ENV>`, `SAPLING_METRICS_TOKEN`.

These are read **only** by `resolveCredential`'s fallback for the first organization, until its admin stores each integration on the Integrations screen. Every other org's credentials are per-org stored secrets. The cleanup phase deletes the fallback and these Worker secrets.

Two naming notes: the Cloudflare account id is a secret on purpose, because a var and a secret sharing a name fail the deploy. And neither Cloudflare value is named `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` or `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`, because the wrangler CLI authenticates with those names itself.

Railway project tokens are **not** read-only — Railway offers no read-only scope.

## Vars (`[vars]` in `wrangler.toml`)

| Var | Production value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PUBLIC_ORIGIN` | `https://trov.dev` | absolute origin for links in mail and MCP results |
| `NOTIFICATIONS_MODE` | `resend` | `local` writes mail bodies to a table and sends nothing |
| `GITHUB_APP_SLUG` | the App's URL name | empty = the App is not configured |
| `SUPPORT_NOTIFY_EMAIL` | `hello@trov.dev` | where support reports are mailed; empty = stored but not mailed |
| `STRIPE_PRICE_TEAM` | the live Pro per-seat Price id | empty = Pro cannot be bought |
| `STRIPE_PRICE_TEAM_YEARLY` | empty | no yearly price is offered |
| `STRIPE_TAX` | `on` | Stripe Tax at checkout |

A deploy sets vars from `wrangler.toml`, so **a change made only in the Cloudflare dashboard is undone by the next deploy**.

Two legacy vars, `GITHUB_REPO` and `REPO_ENVIRONMENTS`, are read by nothing any more. Migration `0042_organizations` copied them into the first org's `org_repos` and `org_environments` rows. The test pool still sets them so one-org test suites can copy them into rows.

## Cron triggers

`[triggers] crons` holds three expressions:

- `*/10 * * * *` — the repo cron (see the Repo dashboard doc).
- `0 * * * *` — the daily digest candidate.
- `0 * * * SUN,MON` — the weekly digest candidate.

Rules:

- `REPO_CRON` in `src/repo/cron.ts` must equal the expression in `wrangler.toml`. A test pins it, because `src/index.ts` dispatches by exact string match.
- Cloudflare cron weekdays are 1–7 or `SUN`–`SAT`, never 0. A bad expression fails the deploy **after** the Worker uploads.
- A change to this list needs `wrangler triggers deploy` after the merge. A Workers Builds deploy does not update the schedule.

## Preview deployments

A Workers Builds build of any branch but `main` is meant to deploy a **Preview**: the branch's code on its own URL, with only the bindings of the `[previews]` section.

- Its own empty D1 database (`trov-preview`) and R2 bucket (`trov-preview-artifacts`).
- `NOTIFICATIONS_MODE = "local"`, no support inbox, no Stripe price, no GitHub App slug.
- It never gets production's database or bucket.

`npm run deploy:preview` applies the branch's migrations to `trov-preview` and then runs `wrangler preview`.

**The trap.** The non-production deploy command in the Cloudflare dashboard must be `npm run deploy:preview` — never the production command. Cloudflare refuses `wrangler deploy` from a branch build, but it does **not** refuse `wrangler d1 migrations apply trov --remote`, which would apply an unreviewed branch's migration to the production database. See the deploy runbook doc: as verified on 2026-10-09, a branch push currently does apply that branch's new migrations to production.

## Local development

- `.dev.vars` holds local values; `.dev.vars.example` describes each one.
- `LOCAL_UPSTREAM` points Sync at a local stand-in for GitHub and Gemini. `STRIPE_TEST_API_BASE` points billing at a local stand-in for Stripe. Both are honoured only for a loopback address and never with a live Stripe key (`src/platform/loopback.ts`).
- `vitest.config.ts` blanks every network secret that `.dev.vars` would otherwise leak into the test pool.

## Where the area doc is stale

`docs/architecture/env.md` does not list `TROV_KEK`, `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`, `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` or the Stripe vars; those are documented in `HANDOFF.md`, `organizations.md` and `billing.md` instead. It also still describes `REPO_ENVIRONMENTS` at length although it says itself that nothing reads it.

trov-handoffs-and-prompts.title: Handoffs and the Prompt Library
trov-handoffs-and-prompts.body:
# Handoffs and the Prompt Library

Source: `docs/architecture/handoffs-prompts.md`, `src/tools/handoffs.ts`, `src/tools/prompts.ts`, `shared/handoffs.ts`, `web/src/handoffs.ts`, `web/src/prompts.ts`, migration `0028_handoffs_prompts`.

Both are **direct writers**, not the ingestion gate. Neither has vocabulary or confidence.

## Handoffs

A handoff is an addressed message for the next session, not knowledge. It is written directly and never staged.

**Shape.** An integer id shown as `#12` (the per-org number), a `recipient` (a handle, or `anyone`), and a fixed `context` object: `{ repo, branch, task, done[], next[], files[] }`. It may carry an inline prompt. It expires seven days after it is created.

**Rules.**

- The sender is always the authenticated principal.
- A create that carries a session id is replay-safe through `processed_items`, the same ledger `/ingest` uses.
- **Claim is one conditional `UPDATE`**: it succeeds only while the handoff is `pending` and the caller is the recipient, the sender, or the handoff is for `anyone`. On zero rows changed it re-reads to answer 404, 403 or 409. A race therefore has exactly one winner.
- Expire is allowed to the sender or the named recipient, on a pending handoff only.
- Creating a handoff also writes a feed row.
- The repo cron expires overdue pending handoffs on every tick (`expireDueHandoffs`, D1 only).

**MCP tools**, for every principal: `send_handoff`, `list_handoffs` (pending ones for you and for `anyone` by default; `box: "sent"` shows your own), `get_handoff` (reads without claiming), `claim_handoff` (returns one markdown block to act on), `expire_handoff`.

The `load-context` skill lists waiting handoffs at session start. It never claims one on its own — a claim is permanent and takes the handoff from everyone else, so the person picks.

## Prompts

A prompt is a reusable, versioned instruction with `{{vars}}`.

- Every save appends a version. The latest version's status and body **are** the prompt's.
- `savePrompt(…, via)` has two callers. A person (the cookie route) may save `draft`, `staged` or `published` and may rename the slug. An agent (MCP `save_prompt`) is **forced to `staged`** and may not rename.
- Publishing a staged version and retagging are session-cookie only.
- **Usage.** `use_count` and `last_used_at` are bumped by one conditional `UPDATE` in `recordPromptUse`, from MCP `get_prompt` and from the web Copy button. A use is not an edit, so `updated_at` does not move.
- `prompts_fts` is a standalone full-text index kept at the latest version by triggers on both tables.

**MCP tools**, for every principal: `search_prompts`, `get_prompt` (fills the variables and lists the ones still `unfilled` — ask for those, never guess), `save_prompt`.

## Deleting a prompt is soft

`POST /api/prompts/:slug/delete` stamps `deleted_at` and `deleted_by` and touches nothing else. Every version stays in the database.

- Only the prompt's author or an org admin may delete; anyone else gets a 403 with nothing written.
- A deleted prompt is gone from **every** read: the library, its own page (the same 404 as an unknown slug), quick search, the MCP tools and the full-text index.
- **Its slug stays reserved.** Saving to it is a 409. A reused slug would silently re-point everything that names it — handoffs, skills, agents' `get_prompt` calls — at different instructions.
- `POST /api/prompts/:slug/restore` brings it back exactly as it was.
- There is no MCP delete. An agent can never remove a prompt.

On screen, "Delete prompt" opens the shared confirmation modal, then shows a toast with an Undo that calls restore.

## Routes

All session-cookie, answering `{ error }` on failure:

- `GET /api/handoffs?box=mine|me|anyone|sent`, `GET /api/handoffs/:id`, `POST /api/handoffs`, `POST /api/handoffs/:id/claim`, `POST /api/handoffs/:id/expire`
- `GET /api/prompts?q&tags&sort`, `GET /api/prompts/:slug`, `GET /api/prompts/:slug/versions`, `POST /api/prompts`, `POST /api/prompts/:slug/tags`, `POST /api/prompts/:slug/publish`, `POST /api/prompts/:slug/delete`, `POST /api/prompts/:slug/restore`

The Hono app stays cookie-only. Agents reach these through MCP, not a bearer on `/api/*`.

## Screens

- Handoffs: `#handoffs`, `#handoffs/new`, `#handoffs/<id>`.
- Prompt Library: `#prompts`, `#prompts/new`, `#prompts/<slug>`, `#prompts/<slug>/edit`, `#prompts/<slug>/version`.

## Skills

`handoff` (explicit only; one handoff per session), `prompts`, and `load-context`.

trov-ingestion-gate.title: The ingestion gate and triage
trov-ingestion-gate.body:
# The ingestion gate and triage

Source: `docs/architecture/ingestion-gate.md`, `src/consumer.ts`, `shared/vocabulary.ts`. Read the area file before changing any of this.

## What the gate is for

Trov has two classes of write.

- **Ingested content** is knowledge an agent proposes: feed entries, doc proposals, ADR drafts, captured GitHub events and repo events. An agent can be wrong, and a wrong doc gets believed, so this content goes through a gate and a person confirms it.
- **Authored and computed writes** go direct. Authored: the plan, tickets, sprints, handoffs, prompts, artifacts, people. Computed: sprint progress, PR and issue summaries, repo metrics and snapshots, the GitHub issue mirror. These are "promote-class" writers in `src/tools/`.

The gate is therefore an *ingestion* gate, not a universal write gate. The rule for new work: a new ingestion path goes **into** the gate, never beside it as a second surface.

## Where it lives

`src/consumer.ts` has one gate function per type: `ingestFeedEntry`, `ingestDocProposal`, `ingestAdrDraft`, `ingestEvent`, `ingestRepoEvent`. Every entry point is a thin adapter over them:

- `POST /ingest` and the MCP `record_session` batch tool, both through `consume()`.
- The per-entry MCP tools `append_feed` and `propose_doc_update`.
- `POST /api/docs/propose`, where a signed-in person stages a new doc through `ingestDocProposal`.
- `/webhook/github`, which calls `ingestEvent` (into `events`, for My Work) and, independently, `ingestRepoEvent` (into `repo_events`, for the Repo dashboard) off the same HMAC-verified delivery.

## What the gate does

It reconciles; it does not just route.

- **Replay ledger.** `processed_items` is keyed by `session.id + item_index`. Re-posting the same payload drops every item as `unchanged`. The per-entry MCP tools use a throwaway UUID session, so each call is reconciled on its own.
- **Content-hash dedupe.** A SHA-256 of the body. An identical body for an existing slug or ADR is a no-op (`unchanged`) unless `force: true` is passed.
- **Change typing.** `change_kind` is `new`, `edit` or `rewrite`, computed by the server with a line diff of the proposed body against the live body. `base_version` records which version the writer read, so a stale edit is flagged. Both are stored on `doc_versions`.
- **Vocabulary.** A section or tag outside `shared/vocabulary.ts` routes the item to triage. Nothing is guessed. Sections are `reference`, `context`, `decisions`, `needs-triage`; tags are `auth`, `architecture`, `infra`, `api`, `ui`, `data`. The file must match `migrations/0002_seed_vocab.sql`.
- **Confidence.** Low confidence on a **new** slug goes to triage. Low confidence on an **existing** slug is staged and flagged (`low_confidence = 1`) for closer review.
- **Doc images.** A doc body may embed only images uploaded to Trov, written `![alt](/img/<sha256>)`. A `/img/` reference with no `doc_images` row, an external image URL or a `data:` URI makes the proposal `refused`: nothing is staged or triaged, and it is not ledgered, so re-sending after the upload works. Code blocks are not scanned.
- **Author.** Always the authenticated principal, passed in by the caller. A client-supplied `session.author` is ignored.

## Events and repo events

Events carry no vocabulary or confidence. An event is an external fact captured verbatim and deduped by a unique `semantic_key` (for example `gh:pr:42:merged`) written with `INSERT OR IGNORE`, so a redelivery or a backfill overlap drops as `unchanged`. An event's `subject_login` is a second identity — who the event is about — and is trusted only after the HMAC check.

Repo capture is a sibling gate with the same dedupe but its own table, on purpose. `ingestEvent` raises an identity task for each unmapped login, which would be wrong for bots and high-volume CI telemetry. `ingestRepoEvent` does no identity intake and no summarising. It is reached only from the verified webhook and from `reconcileRepo` in `src/repo/github.ts` (run by an admin's Sync GitHub and by the repo cron), never through `/ingest`.

In `src/webhook.ts`, `WORK_EVENT_NAMES` (`pull_request`, `issues`) and `REPO_EVENT_NAMES` (`pull_request`, `push`, `pull_request_review`, `deployment_status`, `check_run`, `workflow_run`, `status`) decide which deliveries feed which capture. A repo-capture failure is caught and logged and never costs the My Work capture.

`repo_metrics` points and `repo_snapshots` are computed writes, not gated: `putMetric` and `putSnapshot` in `src/repo/store.ts` validate their own input, and `putMetric` is first-write-wins.

## Triage

Items the gate could not place land in the triage queue. A person resolves each one over session-cookie routes, which are never MCP tools:

- `POST /needs-triage/:id/discard` — a soft dismiss.
- `POST /needs-triage/:id/assign` — re-runs the item's stored `raw` through the **same** gate for the chosen type, then records `resolution = 'assigned'` with `assigned_ref`. The assignable kinds are exactly `doc`, `adr` and `feed`.

Every triage exit is soft. Nothing is hard-deleted: `resolved = 1` plus `resolved_at`, `resolved_by`, `resolution` and `assigned_ref` record how the item left the queue.

## For an agent

- Use only the vocabulary above, and send `confidence: "high"` only for what you read directly.
- Read the doc first and pass its `current_version` as `base_version`.
- Check the outcome of every call: staged, `unchanged`, `needs_triage` or `refused`. Fix the cause rather than resending.

trov-mcp-connection-modes.title: MCP connections: which organization a call acts in
trov-mcp-connection-modes.body:
# MCP connections: which organization a call acts in

Source: `docs/architecture/data-layer.md` § Bearer, `docs/architecture/auth-identity-people.md`, `src/data/bearer.ts`, `src/data/context.ts` (`liveTenants`), `src/mcp.ts`, `shared/repo-ref.ts`, migration `0051_mcp_connection_orgs`. Shipped in release 0.25.

## The idea

A credential names a **person** and a **way of choosing** among that person's organizations. `src/data/bearer.ts` is the only place that choice is made.

Every organization it can come up with is read through `liveTenants`: the person's membership **today**, of an org that is not suspended, with the role they hold there now. Nothing in a request can add an organization to that list. The `repo` and `org` arguments only choose within it.

## Three kinds of credential

| Credential | Can reach | Acts in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A pasted token (`mcp_tokens.org_id`) | the one org on its row | that org, always |
| An OAuth connection, mode **Manual** | the orgs its person allowed (`oauth_grant_orgs`) and is still a live member of | its **current** org |
| An OAuth connection, mode **Follow the repository** | every org its person is a live member of | the org that has the call's `repo` connected |

The consent page asks which mode at sign-in. Follow the repository is recommended and preselected when the person has several orgs. In Manual, the person ticks organizations and picks which one the connection starts in.

## Per request

`resolveBearerConnection` does two reads: the credential by hash, then its reach.

If there is nowhere to act at all, the answer is the single `unauthorized` (a 401 `invalid_token` on `/mcp`). That covers an unknown, revoked or expired credential; a token whose person left its org or whose org is suspended; a manual connection none of whose allowed orgs is live; and a repo connection whose person is in no org.

## Per tool call

`resolveCall(conn, { repo, org })`. Every org tool takes these two **optional** arguments; `src/mcp.ts` adds them in front of the tool's own, and a tool body never sees `org`.

A refusal is an MCP tool error `{ error, code, orgs? }` that has read and written nothing. `orgs` only ever lists slugs of the person's own organizations.

**Manual (and a pasted token):**

- The call acts in the current org.
- `org` (a slug) picks another for this call only — and only one the connection is allowed. Anything else is the same `org_not_allowed`, whether the org is unknown, someone else's, or one the person is in but did not allow.
- If the current org has dropped out while others remain, the call is `org_unavailable`, naming what is left. It never falls through to another org on its own.
- `repo` is ignored.

**Follow the repository:**

- `repo` is required (`repo_required`). It must be a GitHub `owner/name`, or whatever `git remote get-url origin` prints; `normalizeRepoRef` reduces both to one spelling.
- Among the person's live orgs, the ones with an `org_repos` row for that repository (typed by hand, or seen through the org's GitHub App installation):
  - exactly one → that org;
  - none → `not_connected`, with the **same bytes** whether the repository is unknown, connected nowhere, or connected only in an org the person is not in;
  - several → `ambiguous_org`, listing those slugs. The `org` argument settles it.

`admitCall` then runs before the tool body. A repo connection's first call into an org takes one of the person's agent-connection slots there (`requirePlan`, so it can answer `plan_limit`).

## The connection's own tools

Two tools act in no org:

- `get_connection` — the handle, the mode, the organization this call would act in and the role there, a manual connection's current org, the orgs it can reach, and `unresolved` when it would act nowhere. It reads no org's data.
- `switch_org` — moves a manual connection's current org to another it is **already allowed**. It applies to every session sharing the connection.

Switching is navigation inside what the person granted. **Adding** an org is not a tool, and never will be over MCP.

## What a person changes, signed in

Settings › MCP access › Connected apps › **Change organization…** opens the connection's scope as a dialog. Every change saves at once through session-cookie routes:

- `POST /auth/oauth-grants/:id/mode` — switch between the two modes.
- `POST /auth/oauth-grants/:id/orgs { org, on }` — allow or stop allowing an org. Not the current one, and not the last one.
- `POST /auth/oauth-grants/:id/current { org }` — pick the current org among those allowed.

Each is keyed by grant id **and** person, so someone else's grant, an unknown id and an org the caller is not in are all the same 404.

## Staying honest over time

- Code exchange and refresh re-check standing: if the person is no longer a member of any org the connection can reach, the request is refused and the grant revoked.
- `removeMember` drops the connection's reach into that org in the same batch as the removal.
- Connections from before migration 0051 are Manual with exactly one allowed org, so they behave as they always did.

## Admin over MCP, and metering

- "Admin" is `hasRole(ctx, "admin")` in the org the call **resolved** to. `update_plan` is listed when the person is an admin in any org the connection reaches, and is `forbidden` on a call that lands where they are not.
- A tool call is metered in the org it resolved to. A call that resolved nowhere is metered nowhere.

## A limit to know

An org's hand-typed repository name is not verified against GitHub. An admin of one of a person's orgs could connect a repository name another of that person's orgs also uses. The result is `ambiguous_org` — a refusal — never a silent redirect.

## Practical notes for an agent

- Call `get_connection` first if you are unsure where you are.
- Older plugin builds (before plugin 0.8.0) expose tools without `repo` / `org` arguments and without `get_connection`. Their calls act in the connection's current organization. In that case, confirm the org by reading — `list_people`, `list_docs`, `get_my_work` — before writing anything.
- Tests: `test/mcp.connection-scope.test.ts` drives both modes end to end; `test/isolation.mcp.test.ts` is the cross-org matrix, and a new tool needs an entry there.

trov-notifications.title: Email notifications and digests
trov-notifications.body:
# Email notifications and digests

Source: `docs/architecture/notifications.md`, `src/notifications/` (`registry.ts`, `resolve.ts`, `run.ts`, `retry.ts`, `window.ts`, `cron.ts`, `resend.ts`, `unsubscribe.ts`, `assemble.ts`, `invite.ts`, `welcome.ts`, `grant.ts`, `support.ts`), `src/orgs/mail.ts`, `shared/notifications.ts`.

## The shape

Digests are a **read-side projection, never a writer**. They are assembled from D1 and sent through Resend. The pipeline writes only to its own `notification_*` tables.

## Kinds — a registry in code

`registry.ts` and `shared/notifications.ts` define one `NotificationKind` per digest section:

- `my_work` — merged pull requests in the window plus open assigned issues, summarised exactly as My Work does.
- `review_queue` — open proposals and draft decisions.
- `roadmap_plan` — the plan's changes in the window.
- `ticketq` — the ticket queue: unassigned submitted tickets org-wide plus the recipient's own open assigned tickets.

A renderer is a pure read that returns a section or `null`. Null means nothing to say, and the section is dropped. Adding a kind is one registry entry plus one renderer.

## Cadences

`daily`, `weekly` or `off`. **There is no immediate tier.**

Resolution (`resolve.ts`): the user's preference, then the org policy's default, then the registry default. A policy that disables a kind wins before the user layer.

## A run

`run.ts`, per eligible person (an address on file, not unsubscribed):

1. **Claim the outbox row first**, with `INSERT OR IGNORE` on an idempotency key. A conflict skips the person, so a cron that fires twice is harmless.
2. Render the kinds and drop the nulls.
3. Zero sections → `skipped`. Otherwise one message → `sent` (with the provider's id) or `failed` (with the error).

`retry.ts` re-attempts only `failed` rows. Windows (`window.ts`) are computed in the org's timezone: daily is the previous 24 hours (72 on Monday), weekly the previous seven days.

There is one digest per (person, org). Each org is due on its own `notification_settings`.

## The cron

Two hourly triggers in `wrangler.toml` — a daily candidate and a weekly candidate — dispatched by expression in `scheduled()`. The real gate is in code: `notification_settings.send_hour` and `timezone` at fire time. Static cron expressions cannot read D1 or follow daylight saving.

Cloudflare cron weekdays are 1–7 or `SUN`–`SAT`, never 0. A bad expression fails the deploy after the Worker uploads.

## Delivery modes

`resend.ts` reads `NOTIFICATIONS_MODE`:

- absent or `local` — bodies go to a dev-only outbox-bodies table and the mail provider is **never** called;
- `resend` — requires `RESEND_API_KEY`. A missing key is a config error, never a silent fallback.

Digests carry `List-Unsubscribe` headers, including one-click.

The From address is the platform's on every mail path. An org contributes a sanitised display name only (see the abuse-limits doc).

## Unsubscribe

`/u/<token>` is a signed link (an HMAC keyed from `COOKIE_SECRET`). It is one of the signed-token exceptions handled in `src/index.ts` outside the session gate. A POST can **only** set `email_unsubscribed = 1`. Preferences survive an unsubscribe. The unsubscribe is global, not per org.

## HTTP

`src/notifications/routes.ts`, session-cookie only, never MCP:

- `prefs` (GET and PUT) — a person's own row only.
- Admin-only: `policy`, `settings`, `outbox`, `persons/:handle`, test send.

## Where the address comes from

It is seeded at first sign-in — GitHub's primary verified address, or Google's verified `email` claim — through a write that never overwrites a value the user or an admin edited.

## Transactional mail (not kinds)

These have no cadence, preference or window:

- **Invitation** (`invite.ts`, sent from `src/orgs/mail.ts`) — one message per invite or resend. The outcome lands on the invitation row.
- **Welcome** (`welcome.ts`) — sent to a provider-verified address. It links into the guided setup.
- **Grant notice** (`grant.ts`) — tells a person they can set up an organization. It belongs to no org and goes through `platformDeliveryFor`.
- **Support notice** (`support.ts`) — the only mail addressed to the operator, and the only one with a Reply-To. See the support doc.

None of them can fail the request that caused it.

## The look

`emailBanner` in `assemble.ts` is the one banner for every mail. `emailCardOpen()` wraps each mail in a fluid card: full width with a 680px maximum, never a fixed pixel width, with a fixed-width wrapper for Outlook only. `EMAIL_MOBILE_CSS` tightens it under 520px.

## Tests

Tests assert on outbox and body rows, never on mocks: `test/notifications.*.test.ts`, `test/render.notifications.test.ts`.

## Where the area doc is stale

`docs/architecture/notifications.md` was moved out of CLAUDE.md before multi-tenancy was finished, and three statements in it no longer match the code:

- It says the welcome mail is sent from `POST /auth/onboard`. In the code it is sent from `src/orgs/mail.ts` on a person's **first membership of any org** (`neverJoined`), which is also what `data-layer.md` and `organizations.md` say.
- It gives the outbox key as `user:cadence:window_id`. The code's `outboxKey` in `run.ts` includes the org.
- It says the policy is seeded "per isolate". `data-layer.md` says that seed was removed: the policy is seeded by `createOrg` and topped up per org by the cron.

The code wins in each case.

trov-overview.title: Trov overview: what it is, how it is built, and where to read next
trov-overview.body:
# Trov overview: what it is, how it is built, and where to read next

Source: `CLAUDE.md`, `plugins/trov/skills/trov/SKILL.md`, `src/index.ts`, `wrangler.toml`, and the files in `docs/architecture/`. Start here; every section points to a doc with the detail.

## What Trov is

Trov is a multi-tenant **shared context store**: a team's working memory. It holds the team's docs, decisions, roadmap, a ticket queue, artifacts, a prompt library, handoffs between sessions, and a running feed of what everyone — people and their coding agents — has done. It also shows a dashboard for the team's main repository.

The product was renamed from Canopy to Trov. Some stored identifiers keep the old name on purpose (token prefixes, commit-status names); do not rename them.

It is hosted at `https://trov.dev`. Each organization lives at `/<org-slug>/`.

## The one idea: two classes of write

| | Staged — a person confirms | Direct — takes effect now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **What** | docs, decisions, feed entries | tickets, sprints, the roadmap plan, handoffs, prompts, artifacts |
| **Why** | an agent proposing knowledge can be wrong, and a wrong doc is believed | a request or a plan is an act, not a claim |
| **What bounds it** | the gate: vocabulary, confidence, dedupe, then a person in Review | scope: your own lane, or the admin role |

Agents **propose** knowledge and people **confirm** it. Confirming — promote, reject, ratify, publish, delete — is always done by a signed-in person in the web app and is never available to an agent's token.

Every read says how settled it is: `live` (trust it), or `staged_pending`, `unpromoted`, `draft` (not settled, not fact).

## The architecture: one Worker

**One** Cloudflare Worker on one origin serves everything (`src/index.ts`):

- the **HTTP API** — a Hono app, authenticated by session cookie (`src/routes.ts`);
- a stateless **MCP endpoint** at `/mcp`, authenticated by bearer (`src/mcp.ts`);
- the **webhooks** — GitHub's and Stripe's — authenticated by signature;
- the **web app**, a no-framework TypeScript SPA served from the `ASSETS` binding (`web/`);
- **`scheduled()`** — the repo cron every ten minutes and two hourly email-digest crons.

Storage is one D1 database (SQLite) shared by every organization, plus one R2 bucket for binary files. There is no queue, no vector store and no Durable Object.

A few properties shape everything else:

- **Every tenant statement binds the organization's id**, and the database is reachable only inside `src/data/`.
- **Nothing on a render path calls an external service.** GitHub, Cloudflare, Railway and Gemini are read in webhooks, crons and admin-triggered syncs, and stored. Screens read Trov's own database.
- **Unknown is never shown as zero.** A screen says "not connected" or "—".

## The loop: orient → work → record

The Claude Code plugin (`plugins/trov/`) is how the store stays alive.

1. **Orient** — the `load-context` skill fires before work on an existing area. It queries Trov, reads the person's own work and lists waiting handoffs. Read-only.
2. **Work** as normal.
3. **Record** — the `record-session` skill, only when a person asks. It stages one reconciled batch through the gate at the end of a session.

Alongside: `tickets`, `handoff`, `prompts`, `artifacts`, `my-work`, `read-plan` and `update-plan`.

## Who can do what

A person signs in with GitHub or Google; anyone can. A person belongs to any number of organizations with a role in each: **member**, **admin** or **owner**. The **superadmin** runs the platform but has no access to any organization's content.

An agent acts as the person whose connection it holds, in one organization per call.

Organizations are on a **plan** — Free, Pro (paid per seat through Stripe) or Enterprise — which sets limits on seats, repositories, environments, storage, agent connections and AI summaries.

## The doc set

Each of these is a doc in this organization, by slug.

**Foundations**

- `trov-invariants` — the thirteen rules that hold for every change, and why.
- `trov-codebase-layout` — where things live, the migrations, the release notes.
- `trov-data-layer` — tenant and platform contexts; how to write a statement.
- `trov-testing` — the suite, the seed, the tsconfig rule.

**Knowledge and the gate**

- `trov-ingestion-gate` — the gate and triage.
- `trov-docs-and-decisions` — propose, promote, reject, ratify.
- `trov-feed-and-search` — the feed, `query`, quick search.

**Work**

- `trov-tickets` — the queue, the board, agent writes, the GitHub issue mirror.
- `trov-roadmap-sprints-my-work` — the plan, sprints, progress, My Work.
- `trov-handoffs-and-prompts` — handoffs and the Prompt Library.
- `trov-artifacts` — artifacts and doc images.

**GitHub and the repository**

- `trov-repo-dashboard` — the dashboard and the repo cron.
- `trov-sync-github` — what Sync GitHub does.
- `trov-github-app` — how an organization connects its repositories.

**People, access and organizations**

- `trov-auth-identity-people` — the three auth classes, sign-in, MCP OAuth, profiles.
- `trov-mcp-connection-modes` — which organization an agent's call acts in.
- `trov-organizations` — roles, invitations, Org settings, the superadmin.
- `trov-abuse-limits` — rate limits and what a stranger cannot do.

**Plans and money**

- `trov-plans-limits-grants` — plans, limits, grants and gifts.
- `trov-billing-stripe` — Stripe, the tax switch, the owner's checklist.

**The product surface and operations**

- `trov-web-ui-rules` — repaint, switches, skeletons, empty layouts, corners.
- `trov-notifications` — digests and transactional mail.
- `trov-support-reports` — the support form and Platform › Support.
- `trov-environment` — secrets, vars, bindings.
- `trov-deploy-runbook` — how a change reaches production, and the gotchas.

## State of the product

Production is at **release 0.25** (2026-10-09). Three things have been built but are **not shipped**, and are described as such where they come up: hosting-metrics providers beyond Railway (Vercel, Netlify, Render, Fly.io), an embedded Stripe checkout, and a phone layout for the marketing site.

One cleanup phase of the multi-tenancy work remains: removing the old-path route aliases, the legacy webhook, and the first organization's environment-secret fallback.

## How to trust these docs

These docs were written from the repository's own `docs/architecture/` files and checked against the code where the two could disagree. Where they did disagree, the doc says so and follows the code. If you find a doc here that disagrees with the code, the code wins — propose an update, citing the file.

trov-plans-limits-grants.title: Plans, limits, grants and gifts
trov-plans-limits-grants.body:
# Plans, limits, grants and gifts

Source: `docs/architecture/plans.md`, `shared/plans.ts`, `shared/pricing.ts`, `src/plans/` (`state.ts`, `gate.ts`, `grants.ts`, `gifts.ts`, `free.ts`, `summaries.ts`, `billing.ts`, `routes.ts`), `web/src/org-plan.ts`, `web/src/pricing.ts`. Migrations `0044_plans.sql`, `0048_plan_gifts.sql`.

## The model

Every organization is on a **plan**. A plan is a name over a table of **limits**. The rule for the codebase: a per-org limit goes in `PLANS` and is enforced with `requirePlan` — never an ad-hoc check.

The numbers live in one place, `PLANS` in `shared/plans.ts`. Changing a number there changes it everywhere: enforcement, the settings screens and the pricing page all read the same table. `null` means unlimited.

Plan ids are stored and never renamed. **The id `team` is the plan users see as "Pro".**

| Limit | Free | Pro (`team`) | Enterprise | Counted |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `seats` | 3 | the seats paid for, up to 50 | unlimited | members + pending invitations |
| `repositories` | 1 | 5 | 10 | `org_repos` rows |
| `environments` | 2 | 5 | 10 | `org_environments` rows |
| `artifact_bytes` | 250 MB | 5 GB | unlimited | every stored artifact version |
| `agent_connections` | 5 | 10 | unlimited | **per person**: their live tokens and connected apps for the org |
| `ai_summaries` | 300 | 3,000 | unlimited | **per calendar month (UTC)**: summariser calls attempted |

A fourth plan, **Personal**, is legacy: no longer sold or shown, but an org already on it keeps it. It is also the `FALLBACK_PLAN` — an unknown plan id reads as the smallest plan, so a bad value can only make an org smaller.

**Per-org overrides** (`orgs.plan_overrides`, JSON) replace individual limits for one org. This is how a superadmin sizes an Enterprise org. `resolveEntitlements(plan, overrides)` is the one resolution.

**Features** (`PlanDef.features`) exist as a mechanism — `requireFeature` and a 402 `plan_feature` — but the list is empty on every plan. Nothing is feature-gated today.

## One question, one refusal

`planRefusal(state, limit, used, adding)` in `shared/plans.ts` answers "may this org add this now?". Nothing else compares a count to a cap. A write path calls `requirePlan(ctx, limit, adding)` (`src/plans/gate.ts`); a seat is taken through `seatGate`.

The refusal is **HTTP 402** from every route, mapped once in `app.onError`:

```json
{ "error": "plan_limit", "limit": "seats", "used": 4, "cap": 4, "plan": "team",
  "status": "active", "message": "…", "paid": true, "next": "add_seat" }
```

- It is 402, not 403, because a 403 means "your role may not". No role can fix a plan limit, and nothing else answers 402, so a client can branch on the status alone.
- `next` is the one thing the org's owner can do in Trov: `add_seat` (a paid Pro org below 50 seats) or `upgrade` (a Free org).
- Over MCP it is a tool error with `code: "plan_limit"`.

## Seats

A seat is a **member or a pending invitation**, so ten invitations cannot be accepted into an eleventh seat.

- **Reserve** (a new invitation, a person added directly): refused when members + pending ≥ seats.
- **Accept** (a pending invitation becoming a member): refused only when the org is already full of members, which happens after its plan shrank.

The condition is inside the `INSERT` that takes the seat, so of two requests racing for the last seat, one writes.

## Over a limit

An org can end up over a limit when its plan changes or its paid seats drop. Then, always:

- **nothing is deleted and nobody is removed**; every read keeps working;
- **additions of that kind are refused** (402) until the org is back under; removals are never refused;
- the UI says so in Org settings.

## How a multi-org connection counts

A connected app counts once in every organization that holds a row for it. A Manual connection takes a slot in each org its person allowed. A Follow-the-repository connection takes a slot in an org only on its first call that resolves there. So one connection is never a way around an org's cap, and never spends a slot where it is not used.

## AI summaries

One platform key (`GEMINI_API_KEY`) pays for every org's summaries, so each org's calls are counted and capped per month.

- `orgSummarizers` in `src/plans/summaries.ts` is the only place a summariser is chosen. It returns `null` when the deployment has no key, the org's plan is canceled, or the month's allowance is used.
- **Nothing errors past the cap.** The item is stored with an excerpt instead. A later Sync GitHub retries excerpts once summaries are allowed again — at most 5 per batch and 50 per run.
- What counts is every *attempted* call, recorded in `org_usage_daily` as counts and sizes only — never titles or text.
- At most the first 8,000 characters of a description are sent.
- Summaries are **off** until the owner sets the key.

## Gifts: a plan for free until a date

A superadmin can give an organization Pro or Enterprise free until a date (`src/plans/gifts.ts`, `orgs.plan_gift_until`). When the date passes, the org moves to Free by itself with nothing deleted.

- **Give / Extend / End now** — Platform routes under `/api/platform/orgs/:slug/plan` and `/gift/…`.
