- **Expire** — `expireGifts` runs on every tick of the repo cron, as one guarded batch per org. It is idempotent, and a payment or extension that lands in between wins.
- Only an org that is not paying through a live subscription can be given a gift.
- Any other plan write clears the gift.
- A **grant** can carry a gift as a length (`gift_days`); the clock starts when the grantee creates the organization.
- The owner of a gifted org may start paying before the end; the paid plan takes over at once.
- No mail is sent when a gift is given, is about to end, or ends.

## Free organizations

Any signed-in person who is not a superadmin may create a Free org: `POST /api/orgs` with no grant (`src/plans/free.ts`).

A person may **own one Free org at a time** (`DEFAULT_ORG_LIMIT = 1`). The rule is held inside the creating batch, so two racing requests make one org. Past it, the answer is 403 `free_org_limit`.

## Grants

A grant is the right to create one organization on a given plan (`src/plans/grants.ts`, the global table `org_grants`).

1. **Granted** — `POST /api/platform/grants`, naming a handle, a GitHub login or an email. The grantee needs no account yet.
2. **Seen** — a grant is the caller's when it names their handle, a GitHub identity login, or a provider-verified email. `GET /api/orgs` lists usable grants.
3. **Used** — `POST /api/orgs` creates the org, makes the caller owner and marks the grant used, in one batch. A double submit creates nothing.
4. **Revoked or expired** — an unused grant can be revoked.

Every step is written to `org_admin_audit`.

## The pricing page

One pure render, `pricingSection` in `web/src/pricing.ts`, shown as the landing page's last section and as the static page `/pricing`. Names and limits come from `PLANS`; prices from `PRICING` in `shared/pricing.ts`.

- Free: price 0. Pro: $10 per seat per month, no yearly price set. Enterprise: custom, "Talk to us".
- A purchase is a plain link to `/billing/start?plan=team`. The page calls no API and does not know whether Stripe is set up.
- A plan whose price is `null` shows "Pricing to be announced".

## The billing seam

`src/plans/billing.ts` is everything a payment integration calls: `grantOrganization`, `setOrgPlan`, `markOrgPastDue`, `moveOrgToFree`, `setPaidGrantPlan`, `revokeGrant`. Stripe's webhook calls exactly these and nothing else. A plan's price is not stored in Trov: it is a Stripe Price id in `wrangler.toml`.

## Plan status

`orgs.plan_status` is `active`, `past_due` (changes nothing — the grace period is Stripe's retry schedule) or `canceled` (a legacy frozen state billing no longer writes; an ended subscription now moves the org to Free).

trov-repo-dashboard.title: The Repo dashboard and the repo cron
trov-repo-dashboard.body:
# The Repo dashboard and the repo cron

Source: `docs/architecture/repo-dashboard.md`, `docs/architecture/data-layer.md` § Background jobs, `src/tools/repo.ts`, `src/tools/repo-agent.ts`, `src/repo/` (`cron.ts`, `dispatch.ts`, `capture.ts`, `github.ts`, `poll.ts`, `reads.ts`, `store.ts`, `product.ts`), `shared/repo.ts`, `web/src/repo.ts`.

## What it is

The Repo dashboard (`GET /repo/dashboard` → `getRepoDashboard`; screen `#repo`, with tabs Overview, Code, CI, Usage, Planning) shows one organization's main repository: environments and deploys, CI, code activity, usage, product metrics and planning.

It is the same class of read as My Work: D1-only, session-cookie, **never a 500**. A throw yields an empty payload with `degraded: true`.

**Nothing on its render path fetches.** Every external read happens in the webhook, in `reconcileRepo`, or in the repo cron.

## Never guess: three states per section

Every block travels as a `RepoSection<T>`:

- `ok` — something to show.
- `empty` — capture **has** landed, but nothing falls in the window, or every reading has gone stale.
- `not_connected` — nothing has **ever** been captured for it.

Anything that is not `ok` is unknown, not zero. The same holds inside an `ok` section: a `null` figure is unknown. The screen's copy names what each unconnected section is waiting on. "Preview with sample data" swaps in client-side sample data and never touches the Worker.

## Three capture shapes

- **`repo_events`** rows — through the `ingestRepoEvent` gate (pull requests, pushes, reviews, deploys, check runs, workflow runs).
- **`repo_snapshots`** — one JSON row per kind: `prs_reconciled`, `env_heads`, `drift`, `branches`, `cf_polled`.
- **`repo_metrics`** points — written by `putMetric`, which is `INSERT OR IGNORE`: **first write wins, forever**. That permanence is why pollers store only values that can no longer change, and why `putMetric` normalises the timestamp to one format.

## The repo cron

`src/repo/cron.ts`, `REPO_CRON = "*/10 * * * *"`. `src/index.ts` dispatches by exact string equality on the cron expression, so `REPO_CRON` and the expression in `wrangler.toml` must stay identical — a test pins it.

It spreads the work across the six ticks of an hour:

| Tick | Job |
| --- | --- |
| every tick | `pingHealth`; also expire overdue handoffs and expire plan gifts |
| `:00`, every hour | the usage pollers |
| `:10`, every 6th hour | `recomputeAllProgress` (sprint issue counts) |
| `:20`, every 6th hour | `reconcileRepo` |
| `:30`, every 6th hour | pruning sweeps, including `pruneOAuth` |

Since multi-tenancy, each cadence is a **job over units** run by the rotation dispatcher (`src/repo/dispatch.ts`): one unit per (org, environment) for health and usage, one per org with a primary repo for progress and reconcile. An invocation serves units in order from a stored cursor while it fits a budget of 900 subrequests and 8 minutes. A unit catches its own failure and the loop moves on.

After a merge that changes `[triggers] crons`, run `wrangler triggers deploy`. A Workers Builds deploy does not update the schedule.

## Reconcile — the backfill and the self-heal

`reconcileRepo` (`src/repo/github.ts`) is one function with three callers: an admin's Sync GitHub, an admin's Poll now, and the cron's six-hourly tick. So a repo nobody clicks Sync on still heals within six hours.

Its arms each run in their own guarded block: open pull requests (plus the `prs_reconciled` marker), closed pull requests, the pre-capture commit window, deployments, workflow runs, failing-job labels, environment heads, head checks, `canopy/*` commit statuses, reviews, branches, drift. It returns `{ written, unchanged, failed }`, where `failed` **names** every arm that threw.

Each polled item is rebuilt into the webhook's payload shape and put through the same derivation, so a polled row and a delivered row collide on the same key.

## Rules worth knowing

- **Completeness marker.** `prCaptured` is true only once the `prs_reconciled` snapshot exists. Until then the Overview shows merged pull requests and issues instead of a misleading "Open PRs: 0".
- **Recording window.** A week-over-week delta appears only once capture predates the comparison window (`recordingSince`). The CI failure rate is `null` until a week of runs is captured.
- **Environment pill.** A verdict about checks, with health as an override: `HEALTHY`, `UNKNOWN`, `DEGRADED`, `FAILING`, and `DOWN`, which outranks everything.
- **Health.** A standing ten-minute ping of each environment's frontend and API. A reading older than 30 minutes means the cron stopped, and is treated as absent.
- **Commit-status metrics.** Coverage, bundle size and the TODO count arrive as `canopy/coverage`, `canopy/bundle-kb` and `canopy/todo` commit statuses posted by the target repo's CI. The description must be a strict decimal in range, because these points are never pruned. The `canopy/*` names are kept on purpose after the rename to Trov.
- **Drift and branches** are snapshots computed off the render path.

## Poll now

`POST /admin/poll` — session cookie, admin only, never an MCP tool. It runs health, then usage, then the GitHub reconcile, each in its own guarded arm.

- A lock (a `refresh_lock` snapshot row, three minutes) makes an overlapping run a 409.
- The response is 200 even when every source failed; the body says so. It never carries a token, a header or an account id.
- It does **not** refresh issue-derived sections. Those move only with Sync GitHub.

## The usage pollers

- **Cloudflare Workers analytics** (`pollCloudflare`) — hourly requests and errors, read with a one-hour lag. A `cf_polled` snapshot records which hours were actually looked at, so a quiet hour and a dead poll are not confused.
- **Railway** (`pollRailway`) — hourly CPU and memory, with a per-environment project token.
- **The app's own metrics** (`pollSaplingMetrics`) — active users and product metrics from `GET {apiUrl}/api/internal/metrics` on the target app. Trov is generic over metric keys.

A "current" figure shows only while its latest point is at most three hours old. Every log line is scrubbed of secrets **before** it is cut.

*Not shipped:* reading hosting metrics from other providers (Vercel, Netlify, Render, Fly.io) has been built but is not in production. Production reads hosting from Railway only.

## Pruning

`pruneRepoCapture`: health metrics and plain check rows older than 45 days; hourly usage metrics older than 100 days; product metrics older than 7 days except the midnight rows (kept 100 days). Pull request, push, deploy, run and review rows, and the commit-status metrics, are kept forever.

## Over MCP

`get_repo_dashboard` is available to every principal. `src/tools/repo-agent.ts` is a **view** over the same projection, never a second one. Arguments: `tab`, `range` (`24h` / `7d` / `30d`, default `7d`) and `include_trends`. A section's status is never coerced to zeros.

## What must be true outside this repo

- The repository's webhook (or the GitHub App) must deliver every event in `REPO_EVENT_NAMES`. Without them, reconcile is the only source, up to six hours late.
- The target repo's CI must post the three `canopy/*` statuses.
- The target app must implement the metrics endpoint for active users and product metrics.

## Where the area doc is stale

`docs/architecture/repo-dashboard.md` was moved out of CLAUDE.md before multi-tenancy and still describes a single-org world in places:

- It says jobs need the Worker secret `GITHUB_SERVICE_TOKEN` and the vars `GITHUB_REPO` and `REPO_ENVIRONMENTS`. `data-layer.md` says those vars are **read by nothing** now: the repo is the org's primary `org_repos` row, environments are `org_environments` rows, and credentials come from `resolveGithubCredential` / `resolveCredential`. The Worker secrets survive only as the first organization's fallback.
- It sizes the cron against a cap of 50 subrequests per invocation. The dispatcher's budget in `data-layer.md` is 900.

Trust `data-layer.md` and the code in `src/repo/dispatch.ts` on both points.

trov-roadmap-sprints-my-work.title: Roadmap, sprints and My Work
trov-roadmap-sprints-my-work.body:
# Roadmap, sprints and My Work

Source: `docs/architecture/roadmap-my-work.md`, `docs/architecture/ingestion-gate.md`, `src/tools/sprints.ts`, `src/tools/progress.ts`, `src/tools/summarize.ts`, `shared/sprints.ts`, `shared/sprints-core.ts`, `web/src/mywork.ts`.

The rule for this whole area: **no live GitHub at render**. Everything a screen shows is read from Trov's own database.

## The plan

The roadmap has two layers.

- **The plan** — a narrative plus sprints plus a timeline. It is admin-authored through the `update_plan` MCP tool (the `update-plan` skill), which calls `write_plan`. This is a direct, promote-class write, versioned non-destructively: `plan` holds the singleton narrative and `plan_versions` holds snapshots.
- **Sprints** — the `sprints` table. Sprints are the old milestones, renamed in place by migration 0025: same rows, same ids.

The narrative is short: `PLAN_NARRATIVE_MAX` is 800 characters after trim. It is enforced in the `update_plan` input schema and again at the top of `write_plan`, before the first write — so an over-long narrative or an unknown sprint id writes nothing at all.

Nothing about a sprint is ever staged. Migration 0025 dropped the agent-proposed roadmap queue entirely.

## Sprint writes

Besides the plan write, sprints are created and edited by session-cookie routes over the writers in `src/tools/sprints.ts`:

- `POST /sprints` — created `upcoming`.
- `POST /sprints/:id/active` — `true` makes it `in_progress`, `false` makes it `upcoming`.
- `POST /sprints/:id/resources` — adds a resource link.
- `POST /sprints/:id/complete` — sets `done`.
- `POST /sprints/:id/delete` — a **hard** delete in one batch. Its tickets move to the backlog (`sprint_id = NULL`); past plan snapshots keep naming it.

All five are open to any signed-in member, and the same five are MCP tools for every principal. `done` is never set by the Worker and never inferred from issues closing or from every ticket in the sprint resolving. A person completes a sprint.

## Two vocabularies, one seam

The database keeps its column names; the DTO speaks the product's words. `shared/sprints.ts` is the seam: `row.title` ↔ `view.label`, `row.target_date` ↔ `view.due`, `row.start_date` ↔ `view.start`. `active` is derived (`status === 'in_progress'`), never stored. Only `src/tools/` speaks columns.

## The date rules

- **One sprint-date rule**, `sprintDatesProblem` in `shared/sprints-core.ts`: `start` and `due` are each unset or a real calendar day written `YYYY-MM-DD`, and `start <= due` when both are set. It is enforced on every write path before the first write. Reads never validate, so an old non-ISO due date still reads.
- **One overdue rule**, `sprintDueState(due, now)` in the same file: a sprint is due all of its local due day and overdue from the day after. "Due this week" is today through seven days out.

## Progress

Progress is **tickets only**, computed at read time by the one function `sprintProgress` in `src/tools/sprints.ts`: `total` is the tickets in the sprint (native and mirrored), `closed` is those set `done` or `declined`. A sprint with no tickets reads `0/0`.

GitHub issue counts travel **separately**, as `SprintView.issues` (null when there is no cache row), so a mirrored ticket and its issue are never summed into one number. That half is a stored cache, `sprint_progress`, written as absolute counts by two direct writers: the webhook, on issue events, and the cron backstop `recomputeAllProgress`.

**A disagreement to know about.** The `trov` plugin skill text describes sprint progress as "the sprint's tickets PLUS its cached GitHub issue counts". The code and the area doc say tickets only, with the issue counts alongside. The code wins.

## My Work

`GET /me/dashboard` and the MCP tool `get_my_work` both call `getMyWork`. It is a D1-only projection with three lists:

- `previousActivity` — the person's five most recent summarised merged or closed pull requests.
- `todo` — their five most recently updated open assigned issues.
- `tickets` — their open assigned tickets from both sources, six most recently updated, plus `ticketsTotal`, the uncapped count.

Details that matter:

- The ticket list is keyed on the person's **handle** and read before the identity lookup, so a person with no GitHub identity still gets their tickets.
- An unmapped GitHub login gives an empty event projection. Any D1 failure gives an empty result with `degraded: true` — never a 500.
- The screen no longer shows the issue list, so a mirrored ticket appears there once, as a ticket. Over MCP, a mirrored ticket's issue can appear in both `todo` and `tickets`; `source: "github"` marks it.
- The screen (`web/src/mywork.ts`) reads its other tiles from their own slices: your sessions, docs you own, the review tile, and handoff counts from `handoffsForMe`, the same definition the sidebar badge uses.

## Summaries

Completed pull requests and assigned issues are each summarised **once, at capture time**, in `src/tools/summarize.ts`, by Google Gemini (`gemini-2.5-flash-lite`, a REST call). The result is one validated JSON object stored as columns on `pr_summaries` and `issue_summaries`.

- If the AI call fails, an issue gets a deterministic prose excerpt; a pull request gets a marker row that renders "No summary recorded".
- Summaries can be regenerated through Sync.
- They are never generated at render, and they are never treated as truth.

trov-sync-github.title: Sync GitHub
trov-sync-github.body:
# Sync GitHub

Source: `docs/architecture/sync.md`, `src/tools/backfill.ts` (`runBackfill`), `src/repo/cron.ts` (`runReconcileJob`), `src/sync/runs.ts`, `src/plans/summaries.ts`, `shared/sync.ts`, `web/src/sync.ts`, `web/src/sync-actions.ts`. Migration `0046_sync_runs.sql`. Tests: `test/sync.runs.test.ts`, `test/sync.credential.test.ts`, `test/render.sync.test.ts`.

Every sentence the Sync panel shows is built in `shared/sync.ts` from the rules below.

## What a sync is

A sync is for **one** repository: the org's primary repository, read with the org's GitHub credential. An **admin or owner** starts it from My Work. It is a **run** of one or more **batches**; the browser drives it, posting `/admin/backfill` once per batch.

## What every batch does

In this order:

1. **Reads every closed pull request** from GitHub — the whole history, 100 per page.
2. **Reads every open issue.** If either read is refused, the batch stops and **nothing is written**.
3. **For each open issue:** mirrors it to its ticket (the same `mirrorIssue` the webhook uses), records it as an event for My Work if new or changed, updates sprint progress, and — if it is assigned — writes its AI summary.
4. **For each closed pull request:** records it as an event if new, and writes its AI summary.

Steps 3 and 4 are idempotent. An item already captured is `unchanged`; an item with a real summary is skipped.

## Why a run has more than one batch

Summaries are the only reason. A batch attempts at most **5** (`SYNC_SUMMARIES_PER_BATCH`), issues before pull requests. While items are waiting, the browser asks for another batch, up to **10** (`SYNC_MAX_BATCHES`). So one click attempts at most **50** summaries; a larger backlog is finished by later syncs.

When no summary can be attempted — the deployment has no Gemini key, the org's plan has ended, or the month's allowance is used — an item gets its **excerpt** once and the run is a single batch. A later sync fills the excerpts in.

## The closing refresh

The batch that **ends** the run then runs `reconcileRepo`, the same job the cron runs: open and recently closed pull requests, recent commits, deployments, workflow runs and failed job names, each environment's head and checks, commit statuses, reviews, branches and drift. Each part is independent: one that fails is named and the others still land.

## The credential

A sync resolves the org's GitHub credential in `src/github-app/credential.ts`: the org's live GitHub App installation, else its stored token, else (the first organization only) the Worker's legacy secret.

Two places only ask *whether* a sync could run — the status read and the batch route before it records a run. They call `githubCredentialSource`, which walks the same order **without minting a token**, because the status is read by every member's page every few seconds during a run.

## What a sync never does

It never closes or resolves anything, never deletes, and does not poll usage, hosting or health. That last part is Poll now, on the Repo screen.

## The run record

Each run is one row of `sync_runs`, a tenant table: who started it, when, the repository, where it stands (`batch`, `phase`, `done` of `total`), its counts, its failures and how it ended. It holds counts and failure **codes** only — no title, body or summary text, and no token.

| Status | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `running` | in progress; `updated_at` is its heartbeat |
| `ok` | finished, nothing failed |
| `partial` | finished, but part of the closing refresh failed |
| `failed` | GitHub could not be read, or the batch threw; nothing from that batch was written |
| `abandoned` | it never reported an end; shown as "did not finish" |

Phases within a batch: `reading_prs`, `reading_issues`, `saving_issues`, `saving_prs`, then on the last batch `reconcile` and `done`. While reading, the total is unknown, so the panel shows how many have been read — never a percentage.

## The lock

The run row is the lock. Starting a run is one guarded `INSERT` that writes only when the org has no live run, so of two starts one wins and the other gets a **409 `sync_running`**.

A run is live while it is `running` and has reported within three minutes (`SYNC_STALE_MS`). Past that it stops holding the lock and reads as `abandoned`. Nothing is lost: every write a sync makes is idempotent, and the next one picks up.

**Reloading mid-run.** The browser tab that started a run asks for its next batch, so closing or reloading that tab ends the run after the batch in flight. The panel does not pretend otherwise and does not resume a run.

Runs older than 90 days are deleted by the daily cron (`pruneSyncRuns`).

## Routes

| Route | Gate | Answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /api/o/:slug/admin/backfill` (alias `/admin/backfill`) | admin or owner | one batch: its counts, the run view and the summaries view. 409 if a run is live; 503 with no repository, no credential, or a refused GitHub read; 502 if the batch threw |
| `GET /api/o/:slug/sync` (alias `/api/sync`) | any member | `SyncStatusView`: the repo, what blocks a sync (`no_repo`, `no_token`, `running`), how it would read (`app` / `token`), the running and last runs, and the summary allowance |

With no credential, the panel sends an admin to where **this deployment** connects GitHub: Org settings › Repositories when the GitHub App is configured, else Org settings › Integrations for a token. When the App is installed on an account that does not own the repository, the panel says so by name.

While its own batch request is in flight, the panel polls the status every 1.5 seconds.

## Sync, Poll now and the scheduled refresh

Three different things touch the same data:

- **Sync GitHub** (My Work, admins) — everything above. The only one that reads issues and writes summaries.
- **Poll now** (Repo, admins; `POST /admin/poll`) — health pings, the usage pollers, then the same closing refresh.
- **The scheduled refresh** — the repo cron runs the closing refresh every six hours for every org with a primary repository and a credential.

All three write the `prs_reconciled` snapshot; its time is shown as "Deployments and CI last refreshed …". It does not say which of the three it was.

## Trying it locally

`LOCAL_UPSTREAM`, a `.dev.vars` value, points a local Worker's Sync at a stand-in for GitHub and Gemini on the same machine (`src/sync/local-upstream.ts`). It is honoured only for a loopback address and never while the Worker holds a live Stripe key, so a deployed Worker ignores it. `.dev.vars.example` describes it.

trov-testing.title: Testing: the suite, the seed and the tsconfig rule
trov-testing.body:
# Testing: the suite, the seed and the tsconfig rule

Source: `CLAUDE.md`, `vitest.config.ts`, `test/apply-migrations.ts`, `scripts/seed/reset.mjs`, `tsconfig.worker.json`, `tsconfig.web.json`, `test/helpers/`, and the Tests sections of the files in `docs/architecture/`.

## Running it

- `npm test` — Vitest. This is the source of truth for "is it green".
- One file: `npx vitest run test/<file>.test.ts`.
- `npm run typecheck` — `tsc` over the Worker and the web. It is **not** part of `npm test`. Run both before calling a change done.

## A real database, not mocks

Tests run in Cloudflare's Vitest pool against a **real Miniflare D1**. `vitest.config.ts` reads every file in `migrations/` and `test/apply-migrations.ts` applies them, so a test exercises the real schema, triggers and full-text tables.

A second, empty database (`MT_DB`) exists for the multi-tenancy migration tests, which build an old-shape database with data, apply `0042_organizations` and its generated rollback, and compare.

## The seed

`scripts/seed/reset.mjs` is the canonical seed. It truncates the data tables **before each test** in a foreign-key-safe order and re-seeds:

- two organizations — `org_saplinglearn` and an empty `org_b`;
- six persons in the first: four GitHub engineers and two Google-only people (`meilin`, `sanaok`), each with a role and responsibilities;
- the reserved system person `github-webhook`.

The names are fixture data only; no real organization's data is in the seed.

**Add every new table to `reset.mjs`.** A table that is not reset leaks rows between tests.

Per-org counters restart at 1 on reset, so in the seed org a fresh ticket's number equals its row id — exactly the case that hides a "used the row id instead of the number" bug. `test/numbers.per-org.test.ts` deliberately drives every route and tool with ids that differ from numbers.

## No network, ever

GitHub I/O, Gemini, Stripe and the other network clients are **dependency-injected** (`fetchImpl`, `summarizer`). Stub at the `Response` level. Never hit the network.

- `vitest.config.ts` blanks every network secret that a local `.dev.vars` would otherwise leak into the pool. A test that needs one passes its own env.
- `NOTIFICATIONS_MODE` is blanked, so mail always runs in local mode and tests assert on outbox and body rows.
- The GitHub App is configured in the pool with a throwaway key generated fresh on every run.
- `test/helpers/billing.ts` is an in-memory stand-in for Stripe; `test/helpers/github.ts` and `test/helpers/github-app.ts` do the same for GitHub.

Token-leak tests use a long token and assert that no eight-character piece of it gets out.

## Helpers

`test/helpers/tenant.ts` builds contexts: `systemCtx(org?)`, `tenantCtx(handle, role?, …)`, `bearerCtx(…)`, `mintTokenFor(…)`, `platformCtx`, `ensureMember`, and the constants `ORG_A` and `ORG_B`.

`test/helpers/org-config.ts` gives an org its repository and environment rows. `test/helpers/db.ts` has raw SQL helpers for fixtures — production has none outside `src/data/`.

## Structural tests that guard the invariants

These fail the build when a rule is broken, often before any behaviour test would notice:

| Test | Guards |
| --- | --- |
| `test/data-layer.static.test.ts` | no D1 access outside `src/data/`; every tenant statement binds `org_id` |
| `test/isolation.http.test.ts` | generated from the Hono route registry — a route with no entry fails the suite |
| `test/isolation.mcp.test.ts` | checked against the MCP server's own registry — a new tool needs an entry |
| `test/isolation.*.test.ts` | write through org B, read through org A, expect nothing |
| `test/secrets.mcp.test.ts` | nothing reachable from `src/mcp.ts` imports `src/github-app/`, `src/billing/` or `src/integrations` |
| `test/role-gates.http.test.ts` | admin-only routes refuse members |
| `test/render.sidebar.test.ts` | the sidebar's element tree is the same in every state |
| `test/render.corners.test.ts` | every radius has its line in the corners block |
| `test/render.empty.test.ts` | no empty-layout shape holds text, a control or a status colour |
| `test/releases.test.ts` | release order, unique versions, every release has highlights |
| the cron pin test | `REPO_CRON` equals the expression in `wrangler.toml` |

When one of these fails, add the entry or fix the rule it names. Do not add an exception without a written reason — the data-layer allowlist records a file, a function and a why for each entry.

## Render tests

About forty `test/render.*.test.ts` files call the SPA's pure render functions and assert on the markup. They need no browser.

## The tsconfig rule for web tests

There are two TypeScript projects: `tsconfig.worker.json` (Worker types) and `tsconfig.web.json` (DOM types). A test that imports from `web/src` must be type-checked with DOM types, never Worker fetch types.

**So a test importing `web/src` must be listed in both places:**

1. in `tsconfig.worker.json` → `exclude`;
2. in `tsconfig.web.json` → `include`.

Forget either and `npm run typecheck` fails with confusing DOM or fetch type errors, or silently skips the file. Vitest still runs the test either way, because its file discovery ignores tsconfig — which is why `npm test` can be green while typecheck is red.

## What tests cannot tell you

Several integrations have only ever been exercised against stubs. The area docs name them: parts of the GitHub App flow, the Cloudflare and Railway poll query shapes, and (when first built) Stripe. A green suite says the code agrees with the stubs. The owner checklists in those docs are the real verification.

End-to-end checks against a live local Worker exist as scripts, for example `scripts/e2e/artifacts-agent.mjs`.

trov-tickets.title: Tickets, the board, agent writes and the GitHub issue mirror
trov-tickets.body:
# Tickets, the board, agent writes and the GitHub issue mirror

Source: `docs/architecture/tickets.md`, `src/tools/tickets.ts`, `src/tools/tickets-agent.ts`, `src/tools/ticket-mirror.ts`, `shared/tickets-core.ts`, `web/src/tickets.ts`.

## What a ticket is

A ticket is somebody's request. It is an **authored** write: no vocabulary gate, no confidence, no staged state. A ticket write is visible to the whole org at once. Tickets are the largest authored surface in the product — the writers are in `src/tools/tickets.ts`, behind fourteen session-cookie routes in `src/routes.ts`.

Writers: `create_ticket`, `edit_ticket`, `transition_ticket`, `move_ticket` (a board drop), `toggle_assignee`, `add_ticket_link`, `remove_ticket_link`, `set_ticket_sprint`, `set_ticket_parent`, `add_ticket_comment`, `delete_ticket`.

- Every write bumps `tickets.updated_at`, the queue's sort key.
- A ticket's `id` on every surface is its per-org **number**, never the row id.
- Tickets nest exactly one level. A nesting-rule break is a 409 that writes nothing.
- `delete_ticket` (`POST /tickets/:id/delete`) is a **hard** delete in one `db.batch`: assignees, links, comments, history and artifact links go with it, sub-tickets are detached, and the number is never reissued. Any signed-in member may do it; it is never an MCP tool. A mirrored ticket cannot be deleted (403), because the mirror would only re-create it.

## Statuses and the board

Statuses are `submitted` (shown as Triage), `in_progress`, `testing`, `done`, `declined`. `testing` is an optional step, not a gate. The status machine is `canTransition` in `shared/tickets-core.ts` and is never re-declared on the server.

Every move is free: any status may move to any other, including `done` or `declined` back to open. Only a move to the status the ticket already has is a 409. The open statuses are `OPEN_STATUSES`, spelled `OPEN_STATUS_SQL` in every SQL reader.

The board is the queue's default view (`boardView` in `web/src/tickets.ts`); the Table is the other.

- Each column has a saved order, `tickets.board_rank`, written only by a drag: `POST /tickets/:id/move {to, after_id}` sets status and position in one batch.
- `NULL` rank means "no position": the ticket sits at the top of its column, newest-updated first. A new ticket, and any status change that is not a drop (the status menu, MCP, the mirror), resets the rank to `NULL`.
- The comparator `boardOrder` and the placement `placeInColumn` are one definition in `shared/tickets-core.ts`, shared by the Worker and the SPA's optimistic drop.
- The drag is pointer-driven (`web/src/main.ts`), never HTML5 drag-and-drop. Mouse and pen only; touch scrolls.

## Nothing infers a resolution

`done` and `declined` are never set by a PR merging, an issue closing, the webhook or the cron. A person asks for them — and an agent holding that person's token asking is that person asking.

One exception: a ticket **mirrored** from a GitHub issue follows its own issue's close and reopen. A native ticket that merely links to an issue never does.

## Agent writes are lane-scoped

MCP reads are open to every principal: `list_tickets`, `get_ticket`, `list_sprints`, `get_sprint`. Seeing the queue is how an agent orients.

The writes live in `src/tools/tickets-agent.ts`, the **one** place the lane rule is drawn. Each tool checks, then delegates to the untouched writer in `tools/tickets.ts`, so the transition table, nesting rules and history rows are shared with the web.

- A ticket write is allowed only when the bearer's person is **already an assignee** of that ticket. Otherwise it is `forbidden` (403) and nothing is written.
- An unknown id is `not_found` **before** `forbidden`, so the check never reveals whether a ticket exists.
- `create_ticket` is the one unscoped write. Filing is how work enters the queue.
- `set_ticket_parent` needs the lane on both tickets.
- An **admin** may `set_ticket_sprint` on any ticket, because composing a sprint is sprint management. This spreads to no other verb.
- `assign_ticket { id, login, on }` has its own rule, since assignment is how a ticket gets into a lane: the caller must be an admin, the ticket's requester or a current assignee. It is idempotent, never changes status and writes no history row.

Sprint writes are open to every principal over MCP (`create_sprint`, `set_sprint_active`, `complete_sprint`, `add_sprint_resource`, `delete_sprint`), matching the web. Only the whole-plan rewrite `update_plan` is admin-only.

No provenance is stored. An MCP write is recorded as the person and cannot be told apart from a click.

## Tickets mirrored from GitHub issues

ADR-007 as amended: a ticket may link to GitHub work and may be *sourced from* a GitHub issue, but is never the issue itself. Every issue of the org's main repository is mirrored into a ticket with `source = 'github'` and a unique `source_ref` (`owner/repo#n`). The mirror is a computed write from a verified delivery; it does not go through `consume()`.

- **Where it runs.** `handleGithubWebhook` calls `mirrorIssue` on every verified `issues` delivery, so a redelivery heals a half-failed mirror. The backfill calls the same function for open issues. Pull requests are skipped.
- **Mapping** (`ticketFromIssue`, a pure function). A `[P0]`–`[P3]` title tag or label sets priority (high, high, normal, low). The labels `bug` and `question` set the category; anything else is `other`. GitHub assignees map through `identities`; unmapped ones are dropped. Closed as completed becomes `done`; `not_planned` or `duplicate` becomes `declined`.
- **Ownership.** Title, body, category, priority, requester and assignees are seeded at import and belong to Trov afterwards. Later deliveries never overwrite them. GitHub drives only **closure**, through the module-private `forceStatus` — the one writer allowed to bypass the transition table — recorded as the system person `github-webhook`. Trov never writes back to GitHub.
- **Idempotency.** Creation is one guarded batch keyed by `source_ref`. A delivery older than `source_updated_at` is skipped whole.
- **The lock.** The source link is inserted `locked = 1`; `remove_ticket_link` refuses it with a 403.
- **No double counting.** The ticket-queue digest, the sidebar badge and the Repo dashboard's Open tickets tile read native tickets only (`source = 'canopy'`). Sprint progress and My Work count both.

`github-webhook` is a reserved handle with a `persons` row. It is never listed and can never be assigned, file, comment or link.

# Web UI rules: repaint, switches, skeletons, empty layouts and corners

Source: `docs/architecture/web-ui.md`, `web/src/` (`main.ts`, `render.ts`, `morph.ts`, `sidebar.ts`, `segmented.ts`, `tabs.ts`, `dropdown.ts`, `skeleton.ts`, `preview.ts`, `confirm.ts`, `people.ts`, `ui.ts`, `transition.ts`, `trov.css`).

The SPA is TypeScript and Vite with **no framework**. `main.ts` holds state and acts, `render.ts` turns state into markup, there is one module per screen, `hash.ts` holds the routes, and `trov.css` holds the styles.

## A repaint rebuilds the page unless the page opts out

This is the root cause of "it reloads when I type".

`rerender()` runs on every state change, **including every keystroke in a field**. `paint()` in `web/src/morph.ts` replaces the page's DOM wholesale unless the element is one of:

- the `<aside>` (the sidebar);
- a root-level `data-overlay` (a dialog);
- a page that names itself with **`data-morph="<key>"`**, which is patched in place while the key stays the same.

A rebuilt page restarts every entrance animation, skeleton fade, image and iframe in it. Focus and the caret are restored, so the field itself looks fine and the bug is easy to miss.

**Rule:** a page that holds a form, hosts a dialog, or has a backdrop or an entrance sets `data-morph` on its root. Inside a morphed page, a part that must be *replaced* when it becomes a different thing — a tab's panel, a wizard's step — names itself with `data-morph-key`.

Do **not** fix a flicker by turning animations off in the affected region. That hides one symptom and leaves the rebuild. Find the shared cause.

**A dialog that opens over any screen repaints itself alone.** Most screens are not morphed, so such a dialog cannot rely on its host page. The support dialog is the pattern: opening and closing are a `rerender()`, but everything inside the open dialog goes through its own `repaint()`, which patches the overlay element only. That needs a stable structure: an error or counter that comes and goes is always emitted and shown by attribute.

## The sidebar outlives rerenders

A transition can only animate on an element that survives the state change. So `paint()` patches the `<aside>` in place and swaps only `<main>`.

That works only because **the sidebar's structure is stable** (`web/src/sidebar.ts`): every label, badge, dot and chevron is *always* emitted, and collapsed, open and active are attributes and classes that CSS animates. Emitting a node conditionally there swaps it out from under its own animation. `test/render.sidebar.test.ts` pins the element tree across every state.

The rail is 228px expanded — measured, not chosen by eye — and 64px collapsed. Below 900px it renders collapsed.

## Three controls, never hand-rolled

| Need | Use | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pick a value or a view | `segmented()` | `web/src/segmented.ts` |
| Move between a page's own sections | `tabBar()` | `web/src/tabs.ts` |
| Pick one, with no room for a switch | `dropdown()` | `web/src/dropdown.ts` |

Never a native `<select>`. The segmented switch's fill and the tab bar's underline each slide between options, tracked across paints by the control's stable `id`.

Other fixed choices:

- Confirmations use `confirmModal` (`web/src/confirm.ts`), never `window.confirm`.
- A clickable person goes through `web/src/people.ts`; a picture always through `avatarSrc`.
- Never a button inside a button. A card that opens something uses `hitArea` (`web/src/ui.ts`), with the people laid above it.

## Entrances and motion

A screen's entrance is `[data-enter]`, set by `markEnter()` only when the **route** changed — never on a keystroke, and never because a read landed. A negative animation delay lets a rerender mid-entrance join the animation where the old DOM left off.

All motion is off under `prefers-reduced-motion`.

## Loading skeletons

A screen waiting on a read never paints a bare "Loading…" line and never paints its empty state early. It paints a **skeleton**: the content's own containers with muted bars where the text will be, so nothing moves when the read lands.

- **One helper.** Everything is composed from `web/src/skeleton.ts`. Never hand-roll skeleton markup.
- **In the real frame.** A skeleton sits inside the screen's actual wrappers, beside its real chrome.
- **One region per read.** Each region fills on its own.
- **Only for "not loaded yet".** A refetch keeps the content already on screen.
- Bars stay invisible for the first 150 ms, so a fast read never shows a skeleton.

## Empty layouts

A screen that has **loaded and holds nothing** never collapses to one centred line. It keeps its real chrome and draws its content's shape empty, so a brand-new organization can see what the screen is for. (Shipped in release 0.25.)

- **Skeleton or empty layout?** A read that is *out* is a skeleton. A read that *answered with nothing* is an empty layout (`emptyLayout()` in `web/src/skeleton.ts`). A filter that hides everything is neither — it says "nothing matches". A failed read keeps its error.
- **One sentence, one action per region.** The sentence says what appears here and how it gets there. It claims only what the read proved.
- **Shapes are the skeleton's builders.** Each screen has one shape builder used by both, so the two cannot drift.
- **Never data.** A shape is a box: no name, number, date, avatar, control or status colour. Empty shapes are hollow and still; skeleton bars are filled and pulse. That difference is how a person tells empty from loading at a glance.

`test/render.empty.test.ts` walks every screen's shapes.

### The state preview: `?preview=empty` and `?preview=loading`

The owner of a busy organization never meets either state, so any app address takes a query flag — for example `/<org>/?preview=empty#tickets` or `/<org>/?preview=loading#feed` (`web/src/preview.ts`).

- It is a **projection at render time**. The real state is never written and reads keep running underneath.
- **It never sends a write.** While it is on, the one request sender refuses every request that is not a GET before it leaves the browser.
- An amber banner stays up on every screen saying which state is shown and that it is not your data.

## First-run cards

Onboarding, the org picker and the guided setup are one card in front of a backdrop of the real app shell. A step gives way to the next through `morphStep` (`web/src/transition.ts`, View Transitions).

The backdrop is the app's own markup, so every animation rule would match inside it. `.cnpy-fr-bg` therefore turns animation off for everything in it. If "the screen behind refreshes on every step", check that — it is not a rebuild.

The signed-out landing page (`web/src/landing.ts`) carries the same purple banner and is `data-morph="landing"`, with its dialogs as root-level overlays. *Not shipped:* a phone layout for the marketing site has been built but is not in production.

## Corners

Every radius renders at `--corner-scale` (0.4) of its authored value. **One block at the end of `trov.css`** zeroes every radius and then restores each one the app uses, scaled.

So a **new radius value, or a new class with a radius, needs a line in that block**, or it renders square. `test/render.corners.test.ts` fails until it has one. A status dot must be an element, never a `●` character.
